url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: The massive solar storm that illuminated skies worldwide in May 2024 has uncovered an unexpected twist: Earth's own atmosphere may have helped make the storm so powerful. Satellite measurements revealed that roughly 85% of the charged particles fueling the disturbance originated from Earth's upper atmosphere rather than the solar wind. Scientists also detected an extraordinary 40% weakening of Earth's magnetic field high above the planet.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. Scientists say international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals prevented even greater damage, and Earth's protective ozone layer is still recovering.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Global fossil fuel emissions set to fall in 2026, but total CO2 keeps rising
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall in 2026 as renewable energy and electric vehicles gain ground, but rising emissions from deforestation threaten to push total CO2 emissions to a new record. Scientists warn that the world's remaining carbon budget for limiting warming to 1.5°C could be exhausted in less than four years, even as a lasting decline in emissions appears increasingly within reach.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Ocean heatwaves are hiding months of extra warming
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Marine heatwaves may be only the most intense part of much longer warming events, with elevated temperatures sometimes lingering for months. Researchers found that conventional measurements underestimate total heat exposure by more than 150% on average, potentially overlooking a major source of stress on marine ecosystems.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: The end of humanity? What would happen if the Yellowstone supervolcano erupted now
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: A Yellowstone super-eruption would begin not with a sudden surprise, but with weeks of increasingly alarming warning signs such as migrating earthquake swarms, rapid ground uplift, changing geysers, and rising volcanic gases. In a worst-case scenario, those signals could culminate in a VEI 8 eruption that blasts ash tens of kilometers into the atmosphere, unleashes deadly pyroclastic flows, buries parts of the western United States in ash, and cripples transportation, electricity, water systems, agriculture, and communications across much of North America.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: This deep-sea enzyme survives heat that destroys most proteins
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: A deep-sea microbe uses an exceptionally heat-resistant enzyme to turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia at temperatures that would destroy most proteins. Its unusual structure and a newly observed reaction state may reveal an ancient, shared mechanism behind nitrogen fixation and could eventually inspire cleaner biotechnology and fertilizer production.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists stunned as volcano cloud starts destroying methane
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: The Hunga Tonga eruption may have triggered a surprising chemical reaction that destroyed some of the methane released into the atmosphere. Scientists say the discovery could reshape estimates of methane pollution and inspire new methods for slowing near-term global warming.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Tiny aerosol particles could supercharge tropical storm clouds
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists discovered unusually high water-vapor supersaturation inside deep tropical clouds, creating conditions in which tiny aerosol particles could intensify storm updrafts. The finding suggests earlier studies may have missed the effect because they were looking in the wrong types of clouds.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Earth has a natural thermostat and scientists finally know how it works
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists have identified a hidden feedback loop that may explain how Earth has regulated its climate for tens of millions of years. As sea levels rose and fell, they changed how much phosphate reached the open ocean, affecting marine life and the amount of carbon buried beneath the seafloor. That burial removed carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, helping cool the planet.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: A 37-year soil experiment revealed a hidden climate threat
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: The world's longest-running soil warming experiment has revealed an unexpected climate concern. After nearly four decades, researchers found that warming can cause microbes to break down stable soil carbon that scientists once believed was largely protected. That releases extra carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, potentially accelerating global warming.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: New research reveals the hidden pollution left behind by fireworks
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists have uncovered new evidence that fireworks can pollute both the air and water in ways that extend beyond the visible smoke. The findings show that leftover debris, fine particles, and airborne chemicals may affect ecosystems and increase people's exposure to air pollution during major celebrations.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: A popular climate fix could accidentally trigger massive changes to global weather
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: A new study found that not all geoengineering ideas are created equal. Brightening marine clouds over the eastern Pacific could dramatically weaken the El Niño cycle, triggering major changes to global weather patterns, while stratospheric aerosol injection left the system largely unchanged. Researchers say the results are a reminder that efforts to cool the planet could produce unexpected consequences if they are deployed without a full understanding of how Earth's climate works.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: An invisible forever chemical rain is falling across the planet
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: A surprising study suggests that chemicals introduced to protect the ozone layer may have unintentionally created a growing global pollution problem. Researchers found that refrigerants and certain anesthetic gases have generated more than 335,000 tonnes of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), a highly persistent "forever chemical," that has been deposited across Earth's surface since 2000. The pollutant is now showing up everywhere from rainwater to remote Arctic ice, and scientists expect levels to keep rising.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Giant fire tornadoes could clean up oil spills faster with less pollution
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Researchers have shown that controlled fire whirls can clean up oil spills faster and more cleanly than traditional burning methods. The spinning flames consumed up to 95% of the oil, cut soot emissions by 40%, and could help prevent spills from reaching sensitive marine habitats.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Humans collectively produce more than 2 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide annually just by turning food into energy, a 74% increase over three decades largely driven by population growth. Unlike fossil fuel emissions, however, the CO2 we exhale is part of the natural carbon cycle, and scientists say measuring it more accurately could improve climate models.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists discover a hidden oxygen reservoir deep inside Earth
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists have discovered that magma deep inside Earth can store surprising amounts of extra oxygen, potentially revealing a hidden contributor to our planet's oxygen-rich atmosphere. The findings suggest that ancient volcanic eruptions may have helped transform Earth's atmosphere billions of years ago, with implications for understanding life on other planets.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: NASA captures strange waves high above Hurricane Simon
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: As Hurricane Simon unleashed destructive winds and flooding along Mexico’s coast, NASA satellites captured an extraordinary sight: massive atmospheric waves rippling high above the storm. The rare images reveal how powerful hurricanes can disturb the upper atmosphere, creating patterns that are usually invisible from space.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: A 24-year study uncovers a surprising climate benefit beneath forests
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists have discovered that some forest soils are becoming surprisingly better at removing methane from the atmosphere as temperatures rise and rainfall declines. A study spanning up to 24 years found methane absorption increasing by an average of 3% annually, challenging previous predictions about climate change's effects on forests.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: This new concrete is stronger and pulls CO2 from the air
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Researchers have created a concrete mixture that is both stronger and capable of absorbing carbon dioxide. The best formula, combining zeolite with bamboo biochar, boosted compressive strength by 7.48% and tensile strength by 15% compared with conventional concrete. It also captured about 1.2 grams of CO₂ per day in laboratory testing.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Irrigation’s climate benefit could equal 363 years of its own emissions
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: U.S. irrigation produces some greenhouse gas emissions, but new research suggests it prevents vastly more by allowing farmers to grow more food on less land. Without irrigation, replacing lost crop yields could require converting natural ecosystems into farmland, releasing an estimated 6.86 gigatons of greenhouse gases. That is equivalent to about 363 years of current annual U.S. irrigation emissions.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Indonesia’s most dangerous fires are burning underground
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Indonesia’s dangerous peat fires are surging early in the 2026 fire season as a strengthening El Niño and severe drought dry out wetlands that can burn underground for months. These slow smoldering fires are especially destructive because they release far more fine particles and several pollutants than typical tropical forest fires, while thick smoke can make them difficult for satellites to detect.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists detect a surprising shift in human blood as atmospheric CO2 rises
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Rising carbon dioxide in the atmosphere may be leaving a measurable imprint inside the human body. Researchers analyzing more than two decades of U.S. health data found that blood bicarbonate levels have climbed about 7% since 1999, while calcium and phosphorus have declined—changes that closely track increasing atmospheric CO2.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists identify the rare meteorite that killed the dinosaurs 66 million years ago
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: The asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs was likely an exceptionally rare CO chondrite from a distant region of the solar system. Its unusual chemistry suggests that planet-cooling dust and debris, rather than sulfur inside the asteroid, may have delivered the deadliest blow.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Climate scientist who “proved” humanity is warming Earth says government report got it wrong
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: A pioneering climate scientist is challenging a U.S. government report that cited his research while reaching what he says is the exact opposite conclusion. Benjamin Santer and his colleagues say decades of satellite data clearly reveal the atmospheric “fingerprint” of human-caused climate change. Their new peer-reviewed analysis argues the report contains major scientific errors and should not be relied upon in climate policy decisions.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Major errors found in Al Gore-founded Climate TRACE database
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: A new study from Northern Arizona University is raising red flags about a widely used global emissions database from Climate TRACE, a consortium co-founded by Al Gore. Researchers found that the database may be dramatically undercounting carbon dioxide emissions from cars and trucks in cities—by an average of 70% across 260 U.S. cities, with some cities showing gaps of more than 90%.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists turn tofu and cheese waste into tiny CO2-catching beads
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists have developed biodegradable protein beads made from dairy and tofu waste that can capture carbon dioxide from the atmosphere more efficiently than many current technologies. Unlike conventional systems that require large amounts of energy, the new method releases captured CO2 using a simple room-temperature process.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Super Typhoon Sinlaku triggered atmospheric gravity waves visible from space
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: One of the most powerful typhoons ever recorded this early in the Pacific season did more than unleash flooding and extreme winds—it sent enormous ripples all the way into the upper atmosphere. As Super Typhoon Sinlaku rapidly exploded into a category 5-equivalent storm, satellites captured rare gravity waves spreading outward like rings on a pond, visible high above Earth through a faint glow in the atmosphere.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: A hidden pollutant is changing how the world's forests breathe
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: A massive global analysis found that nitrogen pollution can either speed up or dramatically slow the natural "breathing" of forest soils, depending on the ecosystem's condition. The results reveal hidden tipping points that could affect how forests store carbon and cope with climate change.

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cryosp.title: Cryosphere decline beyond safe planetary limits, putting conditions for human society at risk
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cryosp.summary: New research published at COP31 issues a stark warning about the health of the frozen parts of the planet—ice sheets, mountain glaciers, sea ice, permafrost and snow cover—known as the cryosphere. The study, published in Science, finds that human-driven climate change is degrading these landscapes beyond safe environmental limits, systematically threatening the Earth system conditions on which humanity fundamentally depends. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-concre.title: Concrete and steel—or mangroves and forests? When it comes to climate adaptation, nature is much cheaper
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-concre.summary: What's the best way to protect ourselves against climate change? The default is to reach for concrete and steel to build seawalls, dikes, dams and drainage systems. These can work. But they are expensive and inflexible. There's another, much cheaper option which gets vastly less attention. Mangroves, forests and urban trees can help protect humans and their homes, farms and cities from floods, droughts, rising seas and heat. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-earth-.title: Earth's orbital asymmetries share recurring rhythms with El Niño, study finds
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-earth-.summary: Every few years, an unusual warming of surface waters across the central and eastern tropical Pacific—known as El Niño—reorganizes atmospheric circulation worldwide, bringing severe droughts to some continents and torrential rainfall to others. For decades, oceanographers and meteorologists have mapped the intricate internal machinery behind the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), from shifting trade winds to subsurface ocean waves. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ancien.title: Ancient climate records reveal how East Asian monsoon shifted abruptly into cold and drought
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ancien.summary: How does climate change affect the East Asian monsoon? Researchers from Utrecht University's Faculty of Geosciences, together with colleagues at research institutes in China and Belgium, are investigating this question by looking back 250,000 years. They found that, over long timescales, the monsoon system tracks changes in incoming solar radiation caused by variations in Earth's orbit and tilt. But when radiation falls below a certain threshold, abrupt periods of extreme cold and drought occur, particularly when atmospheric CO₂ concentrations are low. The study was published in Communications Earth & Environment. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-unreal.title: Unrealistic emissions scenarios help AI climate models prepare for unfamiliar futures
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-unreal.summary: Accurate, up-to-date climate projections are essential for planning decisions that enhance the resilience of power grids, protect public health, maximize agricultural yields and more. Now, MIT researchers have developed a technique that streamlines the production of fast, trustworthy and adaptable artificial intelligence models for climate prediction. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-.title: Rain may increase ocean carbon uptake more than we thought
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-.summary: Global carbon budgets, which track carbon's movement among the atmosphere, ocean and land, may underestimate how much carbon the ocean absorbs by roughly 5% to 15% because current estimates do not fully account for rain's effects on the ocean surface. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-tracks.title: Study tracks Rum Jungle Mine's metal legacy through Finniss River food web
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-tracks.summary: The environmental legacy of a uranium-copper mine continues to impact the ecosystem of a major Top End river system more than 50 years after the site was closed, a first-of-its-kind study led by Charles Darwin University (CDU) has found. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-romani.title: From Romania to Kazakhstan, summer droughts linked to less winter ice in two rapidly warming seas
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-romani.summary: This summer, with its scarce rainfall and repeated heat waves, witnessed one of the most severe droughts in Europe since 1540. The resulting wildfires across western Europe received considerable media attention, but eastern Europe was also heavily hit, worsening the humanitarian crisis caused by the war in Ukraine. Simulations have shown that such droughts are bound to become more frequent and severe in the future due to man-made global warming. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-import.title: More important than tropical cyclones: Scientists finally track the hidden weather systems behind most tropical rainfall
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-import.summary: For the first time, researchers in Australia have identified and tracked the weather systems that are collectively more important to rainfall across the tropics than tropical cyclones. The work, published in the journal Weather and Climate Dynamics, has advanced a new way to investigate how tropical rain may change as the Earth warms up. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-simila.title: Why similar changes in cloud cover can have different climate effects
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-simila.summary: Marine low clouds over the world's eastern subtropical oceans strongly influence Earth's temperature by reflecting sunlight back to space. How these clouds change as the planet warms is one of the biggest uncertainties in predicting the severity of future warming. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-airbor.title: Airborne imaging explores a mosaic of thawing permafrost
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-airbor.summary: Permafrost in many of Earth's northern regions is thawing, a process that unlocks greenhouse gases, threatens infrastructure, and could alter landscapes and ecosystems. The Arctic and subarctic are vast, and gaining a comprehensive picture of permafrost distribution is difficult, as it requires seeing under the ground. Now, with a new method that can map permafrost from the air, researchers may get a much more spatially cohesive view of permafrost thickness and distribution. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-deep-r.title: Deep reefs provide corals little refuge from extreme ocean heat
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-deep-r.summary: Once regarded as potential safe havens for corals in a warming climate, deep reefs, which lie at depths between 90 and 150 meters (295 and 490 feet), are no longer sheltered from increasingly intense marine heat waves, according to a new study in Geophysical Research Letters. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ice-co.title: Ice core records uncover widespread air pollution from early 20th-century copper production
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ice-co.summary: About a century ago, the Anaconda Copper Mine complex near Butte, Montana, was emitting vast amounts of air pollution into the atmosphere. As small particles of arsenic and other heavy metals were carried by winds over the Arctic, storms eventually helped pull them to the ground, where they joined layers of history embedded in the ice. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-fossil.title: Fossil CO₂ emissions projected to decrease in 2026 amid clean energy growth and Iran conflict
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-fossil.summary: Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026—driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict—according to new research by the Global Carbon Project. The 2026 edition (the 21st annual report) is published in the journal Earth System Science Data. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-farms-.title: Same farms, different answers: When nitrogen pollution estimates don't add up
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-farms-.summary: To reduce nitrogen pollution stemming from synthetic fertilizer and livestock waste, California's Central Valley relies on five data sets to estimate surplus nitrogen. However, most parts of the United States use just one or two data sets—the U.S. Department of Agriculture's agricultural survey and census—to estimate nitrogen surplus. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-.title: Ocean absorbs more fossil fuel carbon while land uptake stalls, 30 years of data show
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-.summary: The ocean has been absorbing carbon dioxide from fossil fuel emissions at an increasing rate since 1990, while the net uptake of carbon by forests, soils and other land ecosystems has not grown, according to a new study led by scientists at UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-climat.title: Climate could force more than 200 million from homes: U.N. migration chief
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-climat.summary: Climate change could force more than 200 million people from their homes even as countries spend billions on securing their borders, the head of the U.N.'s migration body said Friday. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-climat.title: Why climate anxiety makes some youth take action, while others freeze
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-climat.summary: While young people are constantly exposed to news about climate change, their resulting anxiety does not always translate into environmental action. A new study published in Climate reveals that the relationship between climate distress and climate action is highly complex. While worry pushes some youth to seek solutions, it causes others to freeze up. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio.title: El Niño mostly to blame for Indonesian wildfires: Research
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio.summary: Wildfires that consumed vast swaths of Indonesia this year were driven largely by a strong El Niño, fueled by climate change and decades of natural landscape destruction, researchers said Friday. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-climat.title: Climate change has different consequences for the health of women and men
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-climat.summary: The health risks men and women are exposed to and the illnesses they develop vary widely across lifetimes and places. Yet climate policy and health services often overlook these differences. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-global.title: Global climate policies continue to advance despite setbacks, research finds
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-global.summary: The latest findings from the Oxford Climate Policy Monitor, led by the Blavatnik School of Government and the Oxford Sustainable Law Programme, show that progress in Asia, Africa and Latin America is more than offsetting the weakening or reversal of climate policies in parts of Europe and North America. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio.title: El Niño threatens health, too—early warnings done right can save lives
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio.summary: As communities around the world shore up their infrastructure in anticipation of one of the most powerful El Niños on record in late 2026 and early 2027, they need to think about rising health risks, too—and include them in early weather warnings. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-wood-s.title: Wood stove experiment reveals how wildfire smoke helps sunlight regenerate nitrogen oxides
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-wood-s.summary: Wildfires bring to mind a blazing sea of flames. But what happens to the smoke? Anyone observing a wildfire from a safe distance notices mainly the enormous clouds that tower above the fire. These rise several kilometers and then embark on journeys that can extend across continents and oceans. Pollutants from wildfires in Canada can still be detected, for example, at the Jungfraujoch in the Swiss Alps. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-toxic-.title: Toxic Salton Sea dust may trigger lung inflammation and reduce gut microbial diversity
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-toxic-.summary: Though it may not always feel like it, we are a part of nature, and our health depends on the quality of our environmental surroundings. A new study published in Scientific Reports explores a surprising new connection between climate change, pollution and the negative health impacts marginalized communities disproportionately face. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sensor.title: Sensors on buses and trams could make air quality measurements fairer
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sensor.summary: As cities invest increasingly in quality of life and tackling air pollution, accurate environmental monitoring is high on the agenda. To identify health risks posed by, for example, particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide, Dutch cities have traditionally relied on fixed monitoring stations. These static sensors leave blind spots in certain areas and are not always representative of the diversity of the urban population. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-nitrat.title: Nitrate pollution in rivers linked to dry climates, not just human activity
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-nitrat.summary: Nitrate, a chemical compound of oxygen and nitrogen often used in farm fertilizers, can rise to toxic levels in surrounding water under very dry conditions. This relationship has traditionally been attributed to agricultural runoff or human waste in the environment, but new research led by scientists at Penn State shows that a hot and dry climate elevates concentrations of nitrate in rivers and streams, even in areas without urban or agricultural development. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-microp.title: Microplastics found in wild mammals' blood more than 40 miles from human infrastructure
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-microp.summary: Animals, like humans, are taking up increasing amounts of tiny plastic particles. Such microplastics are demonstrably hazardous to many species under experimental conditions, and it is suspected that they may also pose a threat to animals in the wild. While data about microplastic concentrations in the terrestrial environment exist, it has not yet been clear if higher exposure also translates into higher microplastic accumulation in individual animals. A new paper published in Nature now confirms this link. Environment

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: 128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Ancient ice discovered high in Tibet may be more than 128,000 years old, preserving an extraordinary record of Earth's climate that scientists previously thought had been lost. The discovery reveals a rare glimpse into the last ice age and could reshape our understanding of how glaciers survive dramatic changes in global climate.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists confirm global warming is accelerating faster than ever recorded
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Earth is warming faster than ever recorded, with scientists detecting a major acceleration in global temperatures since around 2015. A new study reveals that the warming rate has surged to approximately 0.35°C per decade, nearly double the average pace observed from 1970 to 2015. After removing natural climate fluctuations, researchers confirmed the acceleration with more than 98% statistical confidence.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Earth's ice ages may have been driven by a hidden ocean chain reaction
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising connection between Earth's opposite poles that may help explain how the planet plunged into past ice ages. New research suggests that as massive ice sheets expanded across the Northern Hemisphere, they cooled Atlantic Ocean waters that eventually traveled south toward Antarctica. This cooling may have disrupted Southern Ocean circulation, allowing the ocean to absorb and store more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, further cooling the planet.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: These tropical trees breathe at night to survive drought
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Some tropical trees have evolved a clever way to survive drought by taking in carbon dioxide at night, allowing them to keep their pores closed during the hot daytime and conserve water. By comparing three Clusia species, researchers discovered that this water-saving form of photosynthesis, known as CAM, did not arise through a single evolutionary change. Instead, ancient genome duplications followed by millions of years of genetic reshuffling produced strikingly different strategies, from strong CAM to stress-triggered and hybrid forms.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Amazon study reveals the best strategies for protecting biodiversity and carbon
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: A large Amazon study suggests the most powerful conservation move may be protecting the forests that are already standing. Preventing damage from wildfires and logging delivered the greatest biodiversity benefits and nearly matched deforestation prevention for protecting carbon. Restoration remains important, particularly where forests have already been heavily cleared, but it was more expensive and less effective on its own.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: One Mount Etna eruption took weeks. Another happened in hours
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Mount Etna’s ancient eruptions followed radically different paths, with some magma lingering near the surface for weeks while other magma raced upward from nearly 30 kilometers deep in just hours. Scientists traced the difference to volcanic gases such as carbon dioxide and water, offering a powerful new way to understand and potentially anticipate explosive eruptions.

url:https://bigthink.com/books/beginners.title: A beginner’s guide to falling in love with Russian literature
url:https://bigthink.com/books/beginners.summary: Few literary canons inspire as much reverence, and fear, as Russia’s. The sheer size and complexity of novels like Leo Tolstoy’s War and Peace (1867) and Fyodor Dostoevsky’s The Brothers Karamazov (1880) have created two groups of readers: Those who have read them, and those who say they will read them — one day. For one reason or another, that day never seems to come. Allow us to make the case for why it should. Reading Russian literature is not only worth the effort, but is also far less arduous than many of us have been led to believe. For this guide, Big Think reached out to Rosamund Bartlett , a cultural historian, translator, and author of many books, among them Tolstoy: A Russian Life (2011) and Chekhov : Scenes from a Life (2004). An honorary research fellow at Oxford, she discusses what makes Russian literature so special and shares her personal reading recommendations. Art, life, and death Like mountaineering or bug collecting, Russian literature usually isn’t something people get into casually. More often than not, what starts as an ordinary curiosity inevitably develops into a passion that stays with you for life. For Bartlett, the question of where and how that passion first originated prompts not one but several answers. “Like so many readers,” she tells Big Think, “I was drawn to Russian writers by their unabashed interest in existential questions. Because of the oppressive political realities — Tsarist and then Soviet — their literary achievements were hard-won. After growing up in London, it was exhilarating to inhabit a world in which the arts, and literary works in particular, were of life-and-death importance.” Her appreciation for Russian literature grew stronger through visits to Moscow and St. Petersburg, back when the latter was still called by its Communist name: Leningrad. “In Soviet times,” she recalls, “both were highly atmospheric, unmodernized cities which largely preserved their 19th-century character and physiognomy.” Walking through streets where Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, [Alexander] Pushkin, and more had walked before, she had “the dizzying sense” that one could “almost touch the past.” A painting of Alexander Pushkin sitting on a park bench (1899). The Russian poet, playwright, and novelist is often credited with developing Russian literature. His works influenced later writers such as Tolstoy and Dostoevsky. ( Credit : The State Museum of Alexander Pushkin / Wikimedia Commons) Popular misconceptions One of the biggest misconceptions about Russian literature — one joked about in TV shows like Cheers , Seinfeld , and Family Guy — is that it is needlessly tedious. This is not true — at least, not always. “Tolstoy wrote his chapters like individual short stories,” Bartlett says. “It is hard not to be gripped by the immediacy of his narration. As Vladimir Nabokov, author of Lolita (1955), once memorably wrote: ‘When you read [Ivan] Turgenev, you know you are reading Turgenev; when you read Tolstoy, you read just because you cannot stop.” Likewise, Russian literature is often thought to be uniformly dry and depressing, yet this too is greatly misleading. Though Russian writers can certainly make you deeply sad, many will also make you laugh out loud. “A lot of it is serious, but you only need to read [Nikolai] Gogol’s surreal short story ‘The Nose’ or his novel Dead Souls (1842) to enjoy the richness of his satirical humor. Pushkin’s wit is apparent everywhere, and in [Ivan] Goncharov’s 1859 novel Oblomov , the comic hero takes several chapters just to get out of bed,” Bartlett points out. A final misconception about Russian literature is that it is like an island: disconnected from and counter to the literary traditions of European countries. While many writers may like to think that, Russian literature is, in fact, irrevocably connected to the West. “Until Peter the Great founded St. Petersburg in 1703,” Bartlett explains, “there were no secular cultural traditions in Russia to speak of. The 18th century was therefore a period of intense assimilation of language, art, music, and literature from all over Europe, principally France, Italy, and Germany.” Revolutionary telegrams That’s not to say Russian literature doesn’t possess unique qualities. On the contrary, its preoccupation with European civilization, in many ways, served as the foundation of its originality. “All the great 19th-century novels,” Bartlett says, “were preoccupied with matters of Russia’s national destiny and challenged Western convention when it came to genre. Russian writers arrived at the party late and variously struggled with an inferiority complex vis-à-vis the weight of European tradition. [They] ultimately infused foreign forms with a creativity that made them utterly distinctive.” Part of this distinctiveness is its aforementioned air of life-and-death importance: A quality rooted in both subject and style. “The critic John Bayley put it well when he described Western literature as being so ‘swaddled in the inertia of its accomplishment, the complacency of its prolongation,’ that even at its ‘most urgent’ it still sounds literary; by contrast, the critical dicta of the Russians seem like telegrams exchanged by revolutionaries after a coup d’état has begun, but before it is known whether it will succeed.’” Because of a lack of political participation, literature in Russia was not just an art but a primary outlet for public discourse. As such, understanding the country’s history will help you understand its literary scene, and vice versa. “It’s no coincidence that Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, and Turgenev were all active and produced their best work around the same time,” Bartlett says. “Following the bleak and repressive years of Nicholas I, the spirit of optimism engendered by the Great Reforms introduced in the early years of Alexander II’s reign in the 1860s — including the abolition of serfdom — unleashed an unprecedented creative energy.” Writers wrote not simply to entertain, but to diagnose societal problems and imagine possible futures: Endeavors that arguably reached their climax in the revolutions of 1917, when Russia transformed from a monarchy into a parliamentary republic and, subsequently, a communist dictatorship. A monument to Nicholas I of Russia in Saint Isaac’s Square, Saint Petersburg. In response to his repressive reign, artists and writers produced profound works that gained international recognition. ( Credit : Wikimedia Commons) Golden Age? When people speak of the Golden Age of Russian literature, they typically refer to a period stretching from the rise of Pushkin in the 1820s up to the deaths of Anton Chekhov and Tolstoy, who passed away in 1904 and 1910, respectively. It’s an alluring label and not entirely exaggerated given the enduring quality of the literary works produced in that period. But it’s also limiting and a little misleading. For one, “Golden Age” suggests a homogeneity that does not accurately reflect how much the form and content of literary production in Russia changed from one decade to the next. “After the deaths of Dostoevsky and Turgenev,” says Bartlett, “Tolstoy abandoned his vocation as a professional novelist to dedicate himself to religious and moral causes. Tsar Alexander III reacted to the violent circumstances of his reformatory father’s assassination with repressive measures, increasing censorship.” And while often grouped alongside the authors listed above, “Chekhov was from a younger generation and forged his career with short stories, befitting the era of so-called ‘small deeds’ rather than expansive novels.” Moreover, the label steals the spotlight from other periods of Russian literary production that deserve our attention, too. “In the 1930s,” Bartlett notes, ”critics began referring to the fin-de-siècle revival of lyric poetry — the Symbolists and Acmeists — as the Silver Age. But were these poets really less valuable than those of the Golden Age?” Unsung women authors The international reputations of Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, and other male authors have also overshadowed the legacy of numerous women authors, whose work is now increasingly available in translation. “There’s Karolina Pavlova, author of A Double Life (1848), and the three Khvoshchinskaya sisters — the so-called Russian Brontës.” She also points to Aleksandr Alexandrov, author of The Cavalry Maiden (1836). Born female with the birth name Nadezhda Durova, he fought as a man in the Napoleonic Wars and is acknowledged as transgender by several contemporary scholars. The plights and personalities of Russian women emerge to varying degrees through the writing of male authors. “The under-described female heroines in early to mid-19th century works by Pushkin, Gogol, Goncharov, [Mikhail] Lermontov, and others are often idealized and two-dimensional, while Tolstoy rejected philosopher John Stuart Mill’s call for equality between the sexes and wrote Anna Karenina (1878) partly to prove a woman’s place was in the home.” Elsewhere, socialist writer Nikolay Chernyshevsky’s novel What Is to Be Done? (1863) was a huge influence on subsequent generations of revolutionaries, including Vladimir Lenin. The story featured an active female protagonist who fiercely advocated gender equality. Later, the Soviet Union uplifted some women writers while silencing others. “Anna Akhmatova, who became the undisputed queen of bohemian artistic circles of St. Petersburg in the years leading up to the 1917 Revolution, went on to lead a life of great courage and artistic integrity in the difficult Stalinist years, to which she bore triumphant witness in her celebrated Requiem (1965), a long narrative poem about the purges conceived while queueing outside a prison in Leningrad to hear news of her arrested son. She died in 1966, but Requiem could not be published in Russia until 1989, at the height of Gorbachev’s perestroika and glasnost .” A Cubist-influenced portrait of Anna Akhmatova by Nathan Altman. Akhmatova was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1965 and 1966. ( Credit : The State Russian Museum / Wikimedia Commons) Bartlett’s reading recommendations To guide you into the vast, not always well-illuminated world of Russian literature, Bartlett recommends the following three books. While we encourage you to follow your own interests, we also present them by level of accessibility. Read them in order and at your comfort level, and you will be ready to keep exploring on your own. Beginner: Chekhov’s short stories “I’d suggest a volume of classic Chekhov short stories for their brevity, modern and simple language, and their mixture of humor with lightly worn meditations on the nature of existence. It is not for nothing that a range of authors, from Katherine Mansfield to Alice Munro, have viewed him as the greatest short story writer who has ever lived. Aided by his training as a doctor, Chekhov had superior powers in diagnosing the absurdity and tragedy of the human condition with extraordinary compassion, and understated stories such as ‘The Lady with the Little Dog’ continue to enjoy worldwide appeal because of the universality and timelessness of their subject matter. “As Raymond Carver once wrote, ‘Chekhov’s stories are as wonderful (and necessary) now as when they first appeared. It is not only the immense number of stories he wrote — for few, if any, writers have ever done more — it is the awesome frequency with which he produced masterpieces, stories that shrive us as well as delight and move us, that lay bare our emotions in ways only true art can accomplish.’” Intermediary: Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina “Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina is a rich tapestry of a novel, which — like War and Peace — can and should be read several times at different stages of one’s life. If one is carried away by the passion of Anna and Vronsky’s illicit relationship during a first reading, the next time we might find ourselves thinking about the differences between romance and love , or becoming engrossed in Levin’s search for the meaning of life and his journey to self-knowledge. “A deeper acquaintance with Anna Karenina might also stimulate us to think about how Tolstoy’s dissection of marital breakdown can be construed as a metaphor for the disintegration of Russian society as a whole post-Emancipation, leading to revolution. Alternatively, [it may] encourage us to ponder Tolstoy’s views on the impact of modern European technology, such as trains and modern agricultural equipment, on traditional Russian ways of life, or how the novel is, at another level, a profound examination of Russia’s vexed relationship with the West.” Advanced: Dostoevsky’s The Brothers Karamazov “Dostoevsky’s lengthy last novel, The Brothers Karamazov , is perhaps not for the faint-hearted, which is reason enough to recommend it last. It represents the culmination of his remarkable journey as both writer and thinker, so it is best read after his other principal novels, and also his frequently overlooked Writer’s Diary (1873), which served as his creative laboratory. Completed during his last decade, this was a unique journalistic enterprise incorporating art and politics, non-fiction and fiction, in which Dostoevsky performed the roles of sole writer, editor, and publisher, and spoke directly to his readers about issues which preoccupied him. “The overriding impression we gain from a first reading of The Brothers Karamazov is one of chaos and dissonance, but its complex, polyphonic text is richly rewarding and reveals an intricately organized structure. On the novel’s surface is the murder of a father and the struggles of his four sons. At its heart is a quest to affirm faith in God, reached through a succession of what Anatoly Lunacharsky termed ‘brilliantly staged dialogues.’ Are there some sins for which one cannot be redeemed? Can one subscribe to a faith which allows the suffering of children? These are some of the novel’s central questions.” This article A beginner’s guide to falling in love with Russian literature is featured on Big Think .

url:https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-b.title: Ask Ethan: Can you write a beginner’s guide to the Standard Model?
url:https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-b.summary: For thousands of years, humanity would wonder just what it was — at a fundamental, elementary level — that made up everything we saw, heard, or otherwise interacted with in the Universe. Ideas ran rampant early on, ranging from the notion of elements to a fundamental single root of everything to tiny building blocks composed of a variety of geometric shapes. It was only in the 19th century that we began breaking terrestrial matter down into the microscopic constituents that compose it, like molecules and atoms, that we began approaching the problem scientifically, and scientific progress continued into the 20th and now 21st centuries. Most of us learn in school about the existence of atoms, the different species of atom (known as elements), and the constituents of atoms: an atomic nucleus made of protons and neutrons, where the number of protons in the nucleus determines which element the atom is, and the much lower-mass electrons that orbit around the nucleus itself. But if that’s where your knowledge stops, our current understanding of what’s fundamental now goes far beyond this picture. How can you get caught up? That’s what Logical_Error wants to know, writing in to ask: “What’s a good beginner guide to understand the Standard Model (assuming knowledge only about protons, neutrons, and electrons)? The main things I’m curious about are the properties of these particles and if we can combine them in exotic ways? Would we know the properties of these combinations?” While there are many guides out there, they aren’t necessarily accessible to someone who only knows about protons, neutrons, and electrons. Let’s begin with only that widespread, conventional understanding, and then work our way up to today’s modern frontiers. The periodic table of the elements is sorted as it is (in row-like periods and column-like groups) because of the number of free/occupied valence electrons, which is the number one factor in determining each atom’s chemical properties. Atoms can link up to form molecules in tremendous varieties, but it’s the electron structure of each one that primarily determines what configurations are possible, likely, and energetically favorable. Credit : ptable.com The scientific endeavor to understand what matter is made of began not with what we currently think of as the way to probe the structure of matter (particle physics), but with chemistry. The goal was to see how different components of matter combined together and broke apart, and it was by adding different forms of energy to a system — both chemical and thermal energy — that you could begin to isolate atoms of different species. When we did isolate them, we found that each “species” of atom, more commonly known as elements: came in different weights, but always had the same electric charge to its nucleus, could exist in different stages of ionization, required different amounts of energy, depending on element type, to achieve that ionization, more-or-less readily combined with various other elements, and both absorbed light at certain sets of specific frequencies and emitted light at those same specific frequencies, all dependent on which element was being examined. The atoms could exist in isolation, could combine by bonding together to make molecules, could lose or gain electrons to make ions, could have differently charged ions bind together to make salts, could dissolve in water to make acids and bases, etc. Through the countless possibilities that atoms and their constituents brought up, the entire physical world (and much of what lies beyond it) could be explained. However, despite the name atom, which comes from the Greek ἄτομος and means uncuttable, it turns out that these entities aren’t indivisible at all. This illustration shows 5 of the main types of radioactive decays: alpha decay, where a nucleus emits an alpha particle (2 protons and 2 neutrons), beta decay, where a nucleus emits an electron, gamma decay, where a nucleus emits a photon, positron emission (also known as beta-plus decay), where a nucleus emits a positron, and electron capture (also known as inverse beta decay), where a nucleus absorbs an electron. These decays can change the atomic and/or mass number of the nucleus, but certain overall conservation laws, like energy, momentum, and charge conservation, must still be obeyed. Beta decay always involves a neutron, whether free or within a nucleus, decaying into a proton, electron, and electron antineutrino. Credit : CNX Chemistry, OpenStax/Wikimedia Commons The key discovery that led to this realization was radioactivity. If raw atoms themselves could emit radiation such as alpha, beta, and gamma particles (now known to be helium-4 nuclei, electrons, and photons, respectively), then atoms themselves must be made up of smaller, subatomic constituents. J.J. Thomson’s work with cathode ray tubes discovered the negatively-charged electron, and Ernest Rutherford’s gold foil experiment showed that the majority of the mass of the atom was concentrated in a positively-charged, very small region of space: the atomic nucleus. A few decades later, firing alpha particles at a sheet of beryllium produced a stream of neutral radiation , soon identified as the neutron. Protons, neutrons, and electrons seemed to be all it took to fully describe the atoms in our Universe. But these weren’t the only particles in existence. We flew high-altitude balloons and took particle detection chambers with us; up in the stratosphere, we didn’t just see tracks consistent with atomic nuclei and their constituents and electrons, but also other types of particles: positrons, which had the same mass of electrons but an opposite charge, and muons and antimuons, which were electron-like and positron-like, but hundreds of times more massive. Additionally, radioactive decay experiments suggested the existence of very light, neutral particles — neutrinos and antineutrinos — and if the antimatter hypothesis was correct, then protons and neutrons should have antimatter counterparts as well: antiprotons and antineutrons. The first muon ever detected, along with other cosmic ray particles, was determined to be the same charge as the electron, but hundreds of times heavier, due to its speed and radius of curvature. The muon was the first of the heavier generations of particles to be discovered, dating all the way back to the 1930s. Credit : P. Kunze, Zeitschrift für Physik, 1933 One type of decay stuck out in particular to suggest that there was a substructure to protons and neutrons: beta decays. In all (regular) beta decays, the parent nucleus: remains at almost exactly the same mass, decreasing only very, very slightly, emits a fast-moving electron, close to the speed of light, changes its species (or element number) by moving one element “up” on the periodic table, and, when you add up the total energy and momentum of the emitted electron and the resulting nucleus, you find that a tiny bit of both gets lost; they aren’t conserved. It was as though a neutron within the original nucleus had transformed into a proton, spit out an electron, and either lost energy and momentum in the process, or spit out an additional “something else” that wasn’t being seen. Other hints (ideas like baryon number conservation, lepton number conservation, the conservation of angular momentum, etc.) pointed toward what that something else might be: a light, fast-moving, neutral, antimatter version of a lepton, an antineutrino. The big question, of course, was how was all of this happening? What was going on inside protons and neutrons to drive these processes? While the antineutrino was finally directly detected back in 1956, more than a quarter-century after it was hypothesized, a new idea came about for probing the proton and neutron for internal structures: the idea of high-energy collider physics. The idea of a de Broglie wave is that every matter particle can also exhibit wavelike behavior, with the properties of the wave given by quantities like momentum and energy of the system. Everything, from electrons to human beings, behave like a wave under the proper conditions. The lower in momentum (i.e., the combination of velocity and mass) a particle is, the longer its de Broglie wavelength is. Credit : Maschen/Wikimedia Commons There are two key aspects to understanding a particle collider. The first is the notion of a matter wave, also known as a de Broglie wave . In quantum physics, it’s well-known that light can behave as both a wave and a particle: propagating through space like a wave, but interacting like a particle when it encounters another quantum. One key to waves — in physics — is that when the wavelength of something is longer than the thing you’re trying to interact with, the wave passes right through. (This is why interstellar dust blocks visible light, but is transparent to longer-wavelength infrared light.) Another key is that the wavelength of any wave, whether a light wave or a matter wave, gets shorter if your wave has higher energies. Therefore, to probe smaller and smaller scales, we need higher and higher energy particles. The second is to understand Einstein’s most famous equation: E = mc² . If you take two particles and collide them together, there’s going to be a certain amount of energy, E, that’s left over after you account for both the rest-mass of all of the particles and the necessary kinetic energy that’s required to conserve the momentum between all of the incoming and outgoing particles. That leftover energy, known as the center-of-mass (or center-of-momentum) energy, is available to potentially create new particles, including new particle-antiparticle pairs, as long as all of the necessary quantum properties (charge, momentum, angular momentum, etc.) remain conserved overall. A proton isn’t just three quarks and gluons, but a sea of dense particles and antiparticles inside. The more precisely we look at a proton and the greater the energies that we perform deep inelastic scattering experiments at, the more substructure we find inside the proton itself. There appears to be no limit to the density of particles inside; it increases without bound as the collision energy rises. Credit : Jim Pivarski/Fermilab/CMS Collaboration It took a certain amount of energy to crack open the atomic nucleus, and reveal the individual protons and neutrons inside. At slightly higher energies, we began to crack open individual protons and neutrons: a technique known as deep inelastic scattering. Above about 200 to 300 MeV in energy — around 20% to 30% the rest mass energy of a proton — you begin penetrating inside a proton itself. The result of these experiments leads to the production of new particles: not necessarily fundamental particles, but particles of a kind that had never been seen before, mesons . Mesons don’t live very long, but the longest lived among them are the pions and the kaons , which can live for up to a few dozen nanoseconds. When they decay, the kaons typically decay to pions, while the pions typically decay to muons (and neutrinos/antineutrinos), while the muons in turn decay into electrons/positrons (and neutrino-antineutrino combinations). Quantities that are observed to be conserved include: electric charge, lepton number, baryon number, linear momentum, angular momentum (including both spin angular momentum and orbital angular momentum), and lepton family number (where the electron family, muon family, and tau family represent the three families). Protons and neutrons are baryons; electrons, muons, taus, and neutrinos are leptons; the mesons are neither, and particles like the photon are neither. The particle tracks emanating from a high energy collision at the LHC in 2012 show the creation of many new particles. By building a sophisticated detector around the collision point of relativistic particles, the properties of what occurred and was created at the collision point can be reconstructed, but what’s created is limited by the available energy from the kinetic energy of the colliding particles, with new particles capable of being created from that available energy, limited by Einstein’s E = mc². The maximum LHC energies are nearly a factor of a trillion (10^12) lower than the energies present at the start of the hot Big Bang. Credit : Panos Charitos/Wikimedia Commons user PCharito With higher and higher energy experiments, as well as evermore sensitive detectors, we began to create more exotic particles: heavier and shorter-lived baryons and mesons, most of which possess more complicated decay pathways than the relatively simple pions and kaons. We created neutral pions and kaons as well as the eta, eta prime, and rho mesons. We created exotic baryons like the lambdas, the sigmas, the xis, and the omega particle. We created resonance-based particles that only lived for a yoctosecond ( 10 -24 seconds), as well as the electron’s and muon’s even heavier sibling: the tau. This created what was known for a long time as a “zoo” of elementary particles. There were all sorts of models that theorists were concocting to try to simplify the enormous numbers of particles that were being created by colliders. One idea was that the pions were combinations of protons, antiprotons, neutrons, and antineutrons that lost most of their mass due to binding energy: the Sakata model . Another was that the heavier baryons, heavier mesons, and heavier leptons were just excited states of the lighter particles like protons, neutrons, and electrons, but that conflicted with the “missing energy” in lepton decays and the idea of lepton family number conservation. Finally, two ideas emerged that wound up being equivalent: the parton model for the interior of baryons and mesons, and the quark model for the substructure of those same particles. The strong force, operating as it does because of the existence of ‘color charge’ and the exchange of gluons, is responsible for the force that holds atomic nuclei together. This force, governed by the exchange of massive gluons, is bounded by the speed of light; from inside a black hole’s event horizon, there’s no way that a force such as this can prevent any outermore particle from reaching the central singularity. Credit : Qashqaiilove/Wikimedia Commons The big idea was that there are, within the proton and neutron, fractionally charged particles — up and down quarks — that move around inside, and are bound together by a new force in addition to the common gravitational and electromagnetic force: the strong nuclear force. Unlike gravity and electromagnetism, which exhibit the most forceful attractions (or repulsions) when two “charges” are closest together, in the case of the strong nuclear force, it behaves more like a spring. When two charges are close together, the force between them drops to zero, like a spring that’s completely unstretched. As the charges move farther apart, though, the force increases, and this is what keeps the quarks, particles with a new kind of “color charge,” confined inside these baryons and mesons. In addition to gravitation, electromagnetism, and the strong nuclear force, there’s also the weak nuclear force, which is the force responsible for radioactive decays. This is the only force that allows particles (quarks and leptons) to change species from one to another. Changes include: transforming a down quark into an up quark, an electron, and an antielectron neutrino, transforming a positively-charged muon into a positron, an electron neutrino, and a muon antineutrino, having a neutral kaon, which contains a strange quark, decay into two pions, or having a negatively charged pion decay into a negatively charged muon and a muon antineutrino. It turns out that, observationally, we have three generations of quarks and leptons (up, down, strange, charm, bottom, and top for the quarks, and electron, muon, and tau particles, plus a related neutrino, for the leptons), as well as gluons, W-and-Z bosons, and the photon for the bosons. In addition to all of those, we also have the Higgs boson : the only “spinless” particle in the Standard Model. This chart shows the fundamental particles of the Standard Model, as well as several examples of composite particles: baryons, antibaryons, and mesons. The fundamental particles are divided up into quarks and leptons, with each quark coming in three color varieties and the leptons consisting of the charged (electron, muon, tau) varieties as well as the neutral (neutrino) varieties. Each of the quarks and leptons also has an antiparticle counterpart. The forces are mediated by bosons, which include eight gluons, the photon, the W-and-Z bosons, and also, separately, the Higgs boson. The graviton is theorized to exist, but is not typically included as a part of the Standard Model. Credit: P. Carlos Budassi and E. Siegel, in preparation The most important, and not necessarily intuitive, way that particles combine in the Standard Model deals with combinations of quarks and/or antiquarks: into baryons, antibaryons, and mesons, or particles that we collectively call hadrons. Each of the quarks has a color assigned to it: think of them as red, green, and blue. If you add all three colors together, you get white, which is colorless. (That’s what baryons are, with protons and neutrons being the most famous baryons.) Similarly, each of the antiquarks has an anticolor assigned to it: cyan, magenta, and yellow. If you add all three anticolors together, you get a colorless combination also. (This makes antibaryons, like antiprotons — which were originally called “negatrons” — and antineutrons.) And, of course, you can add a color and its anticolor together to make a colorless combination: that’s what a meson, like a pion or kaon, is. If you had the idea to ask whether you can combine: two quarks and two antiquarks, four quarks and one antiquark, or six quarks, the answer is yes: these are tetraquark, pentaquark, and hexaquark states, which are theorized to exist and for which some pretty good experimental evidence now exists. The heavier your quarks and the more particles you cram in there, the shorter-lived and more unstable your composite particles are, but you can indeed build them. This chart shows, on a logarithmic scale (with a gap to account for the extreme mass differences of the neutrinos from the other particles) all of the particles of the Standard Model. The electron is several hundred thousand times lighter than the top quark, but the neutrinos are several million times lighter than the electron is. The photon and the gluons are the only massless particles known. Credit: P. Carlos Budassi and E. Siegel, in preparation That’s your introduction to what the Standard Model is! We can measure the rest masses of these Standard Model particles — and, in fact, have measured them all quite well — and there’s an enormous hierarchy there. The photon and gluons are massless, and the three species of neutrino are all incredibly light: somewhere in the ballpark of a tenth of an electron-volt ( 0.1 eV , in energy equivalence) each. The next lightest particle is the electron at 511 keV, followed by the up quark, down quark, muon, strange quark, charm quark, tau, and bottom quark up at 4.7 GeV. The heaviest particles are the W-bosons (80.4 GeV), Z-boson (91.2 GeV), Higgs boson (125.1 GeV), and top quark (173 GeV). The Standard Model very well explains the fundamental particles that exist and the force relationships between them, but it doesn’t explain everything. Among the things that the Standard Model doesn’t explain are: why the particles have the rest masses that they do, what dark matter is, why we have dark energy at all, how our Universe came to have more matter (baryons and charged leptons) than antimatter, and how gravity fits into the big picture with the other known forces. The Standard Model, completed theoretically in the early 1970s and completed observationally in 2012 with the discovery of the Higgs boson, is the rock-solid foundation of modern particle physics, and the most correct and comprehensive description of reality ever concocted by humanity. Someday, we hope to go beyond it, but for now, this is the up-to-the-frontier “start line” where all of our next steps begin. Send in your Ask Ethan questions to startswithabang at gmail dot com !
