url:https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-b.title: A “theory” has a special meaning in science
url:https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-b.summary: Whenever someone tells you that they “have a theory,” you’re probably a mix of curious and skeptical, and with good reason. Most often, you’re going to hear a wild tale that’s a mix of true and dubious facts, possible but suspicious links between them, guesses that range from informed hypotheses to extravagant speculations, and a story about how they’ve introduced one (or more) modifications to the standard story of how things are known to work. This is almost always followed with an important caveat at the end: that they have no proof of this, as it’s “only a theory.” In common, informal use, the word theory is tossed around as casually as words like: hypothesis, guess, hunch, idea, or gut feeling, among others. In other words, when someone shares their pet theory with you in this regard, you might humor them by considering it, but you’d be well within the bounds of reasons to dismiss their “theory” without putting too much weight behind it. But some people take this informal definition of theory — as a mere hypothesis, guess, or idea — and apply it to our most vaunted of scientific theories as well. They’ll argue that Darwinian evolution, the Big Bang, gravitation, and quantum mechanics are just “theories” as well, and therefore shouldn’t be taken to be facts. They’ll argue that theories were overturned in the past, and so they’re justified in not believing today’s theories that are well-accepted as part of the scientific consensus. Some will even point to now-discredited scientific ideas, like the theory of phlogiston, Jungian psychology, or the Lamarckian theory of evolution, or to speculative ideas that have “theory” in the title, like Grand Unified Theory or string theory, to argue that many of our best, currently-accepted theories will eventually turn out to be wrong. But this is a fundamentally dishonest argument, as any scientist will be quick to realize. Here’s what everyone should know about what the word “theory” truly means: in everyday conversation, in scientific circles, in mathematics, and beyond. This animation shows the breakup of supercontinent Gondwanaland, which itself was a large subsection of Pangaea at one point, into the smaller continents of South America, Antarctica, Africa, Australia, as well as components of other continents that are recognizable, such as Arabia and India. The theory of plate tectonics and continental drift is so successful because of the evidence that supports it. Credit : B. Goldberg/Quora, modified by E. Siegel The colloquial use of “theory” is just an “idea” In our everyday life, the word “theory” that we hear bandied about is simply the same as the word “idea.” We make no distinction between whether that idea is: a good one that has merit or a bad one that is contradicted by reality, an old one that was long ago formulated by someone else or a novel one, a valid one that has successful explanatory power or an invalid one that makes incorrect predictions, or a scientific one that can be tested and either verified and validated or contradicted and ruled out, or a non-scientific, unfalsifiable one. In our everyday life, we all have that friend, neighbor, or relative who has rather kooky ideas — something akin to “the Moon is a hologram” or “a secret race of lizard people is controlling the Earth” — and likely refers to their idea as a theory, just as surely as scientists refer to Einstein’s relativity as a theory. The much-ballyhooed idea of panpsychism , although often called a theory, falls into this category of an untestable notion with no evidence behind it. In all of these cases, we’re only talking about an idea: the initial germ of a hypothesis. Hypotheses may yet grow into fully-fledged scientific theories, and indeed what eventually become scientific theories typically start off as mere hypotheses or ideas, but simply having an idea doesn’t mean you have a good idea, a valid idea, or even a scientific idea, much less a scientific theory. In order to go from an idea to a scientific theory, there are multiple ways the idea in question must be scrutinized. Touted as UFO lights, this 2011 photograph over Liverpool does, in fact, document a series of lights in an oddly unnatural-appearing configuration, but this is by no means compelling evidence for aliens. In fact, it’s simply an image looking up at the lights of Radio City Tower under dark, foggy conditions, which does not constitute scientific evidence for either UFOs or aliens. Credit : dreese/Wikimedia Commons Is the idea plausible? Based on what we already know, if this idea turned out to be correct, would it undermine or conflict with observations, measurements, and data that we already possess? If so, then the idea — at least, the idea as it currently stands — is not plausible, and that’s a non-starter for it becoming a scientific theory. Does the idea have explanatory power? Based on the idea you’re considering, are there phenomena, measurements, or observations that are presently not explained by what we know, that could be explained by this new idea? If not, then this idea has no hope of becoming a scientific theory, as “predictive power” is the key reason and motivation for the formulation of scientific theories in the first place. Is the idea testable? This is, in many regards, the biggest one: is there some definitive test that can be performed to test this new idea? Is there some way we can compare this idea to the currently favored, prevailing scientific theory it’s seeking to supplant or replace, where we can put these predictions side-by-side, where they’ll differ from one another, and where nature itself will be the arbiter? If not — if this idea is not scientifically testable — then there never was any scientific merit to it at all. (It doesn’t have to be a “practical with current technology” test, but it does have to be a “possible given the constraints and physical limitations of our Universe” test.) There are other facets to this idea that might appear nice on the surface — whether the idea is elegant, natural, simple , etc. — but it’s really only these three points of plausibility, explanatory power, and testability that make an idea scientific or not. Unless you can test and evaluate this idea based on the evidence you can gather, the measurements you can make, the experiments you can perform and the observations you can undertake, it is not a scientific idea. This four-panel animation shows the individual galaxies present within Abell 2744, Pandora’s Cluster, alongside the X-ray data from Chandra (red) and the lensing map constructed from gravitational lensing data (blue). The mismatch between the X-rays and the lensing map, as shown across a wide variety of X-ray emitting galaxy clusters, is one of the strongest indicators favoring the presence of dark matter. The Bullet Cluster, as well as other galaxy clusters, exhibit similar features. Credit : X-ray: NASA/CXC/ITA/INAF/J.Merten et al, Lensing: NASA/STScI; NAOJ/Subaru; ESO/VLT, Optical: NASA/STScI/R.Dupke; Animation by E. Siegel All scientific theories exist within a “framework” for exploration There are a great many ideas that never make it to the “accepted, valid scientific theory” state, but that nevertheless wind up with the word “theory” attached to them. That’s because, well before something is sufficiently tested to know whether it’s valid or invalid, we have to tease out its consequences so that we know what to look for in terms of evaluating it. This comes during a “theory development” stage. Science, after all, is both: a body of facts, including the full suite of all relevant data that’s ever been gathered about a particular topic, and the process of exploration, where we go down experimental and observational paths whose destination is uncertain, and where nature has ample opportunity to validate and confirm your ideas, to invalidate or refute your ideas, or to surprise you entirely. That’s why it’s so important that we create frameworks where these various ideas can be tested up against one another, directly. Famous examples where we can do this include: the theory that the Earth is flat versus the theory that the Earth is spheroidal, the theory that our Solar System is geocentric versus the theory that it’s heliocentric, the theory that evolution is based on the use-and-disuse of traits (Lamarckian) or based on the combination of mutations/variations and natural selection (Darwinian), or the theory that the Universe exists in a steady, unchanging state versus the theory that the Universe began with a hot Big Bang and has been expanding, cooling, and evolving ever since. The key, in all of these cases, is specificity: a scientific theory is specific about its predictions, and those predictions can be validated or invalidated by actual data that is measurable and observable. One of the great puzzles of the 1500s was how planets moved in an apparently retrograde fashion. This could either be explained through Ptolemy’s geocentric model (left), or Copernicus’ heliocentric one (right). However, getting the details right to arbitrary precision was something neither one could do. It would not be until Kepler’s notion of heliocentric, elliptical orbits, and the subsequent mechanism of gravitation proposed by Newton, that heliocentrism would triumph by scientific standards. Credit : E. Siegel/Beyond the Galaxy In order to work out the consequences of your initial idea or hypothesis, we need to create a framework for testing the idea/hypothesis against the alternatives. This must be based on observation, measurement, and/or experiment; it cannot be a purely intellectual exercise that occurs only in our imaginations. The ability to conduct that translation — from the sandbox of our minds to the hard reality of experiment and observation — is why a testable framework is so important. Today, the key observations supporting: a spheroidal Earth, a heliocentric Solar System, a Darwinian perspective on evolution, and a cosmological hot Big Bang are overwhelming, and that’s why those theories have stood the test of time and remain accepted today. The alternative proposals have fallen away into the trashcan of science history, and while contrarians often attempt to revive them in modified form, the prevailing theories have continued to beat back such challenges. However, it’s important to remember that new theories — and in some cases, modified and resurrected variants of old theories — continuously arise in the scientific literature. The theory that there’s a massive “Planet Nine” out there beyond Neptune, distinct from the more typical, puny bodies in the Kuiper belt or Oort cloud, remains an active area of interest, but until the key evidence supporting its existence arrives (it has yet to do so), this will remain a speculative hypothesis, rather than an accepted scientific theory. Many planetary systems are known where a massive, distant planet orbits far from its parent star. Here in our own Solar System, the hypothesis has been floated that such an object, a “Planet Nine,” exists far out beyond Neptune. However, it has not been found, and the indirect evidence supporting its presence has been seriously called into doubt by the results of the OSSOS (Outer Solar System Origins Survey) collaboration. Credit : ESA/Hubble, M. Kornmesser Only validated models that accurately describe reality better than the alternatives become full-fledged, validated scientific theories This is what happens to the absolute “best of the best” of ideas in science: they become accepted scientific theories. Einstein’s general theory of relativity is one such example, as is the quantum theory of particles and fields in the Standard Model. This happened in biology for the theory of Darwinian evolution (inheritance of traits and the evolutionary mechanism of natural selection), in medicine for the germ theory of disease, in chemistry for the theory of atoms, and in many other arenas: where one idea made successful predictions that were borne out and validated by observation and experiment — by a huge suite of robust scientific data — whereas their alternatives failed in one or more ways. This only occurs when you have an initial idea that was plausible, with explanatory and predictive power, and that has unique features that differentiate it from other, alternative, rival ideas. This furthermore only occurs when the idea is formulated under a framework that allows observable, measurable, quantitative consequences to be derived from that idea, and when those consequences and predictions are then put to the critical test in every way possible, and pass those tests every time and in every way. When we talk about our accepted scientific theories of the day, this is the space in which they all live. In biology, organisms inherit traits from their parent organism(s), with the only differences coming from mutations and, if there’s more than one parent, a combination of the genetic information present in both parents’ genomes. Darwinian evolution explains how evolution by natural selection works, but genetics, and more recently, DNA, more fully describe the mechanisms behind that evolutionary process. Credit: ktsdesign via Adobe Stock There are a great many people — scientists chief among them — who are eager to challenge these accepted theories, also known as the “consensus position” in science. There are even a great many scientists who very, very strongly believe that the consensus position will not hold for long, and that a new, superior theory will come along that overturns that accepted theory. Some of them even think that their pet ideas or hypotheses will be the one to do it. But there’s a 3-step formula that every successful scientific revolution has followed , and whatever scientific revolution you’re attempting to instigate must follow as well. That formula is: Step 1: Your new theory must reproduce all the successes of the leading theory . Whatever the currently accepted theory successfully predicts, describes, and explains, your new theory must successfully predict, describe, and explain as well. Step 2: Your new theory must succeed where the prior theory does not . Every theory has what can be thought of as a “range of validity,” where within that range, its predictions agree with reality, but outside of that range, either its predictions are invalid, untested, or flat-out disagree with what we observe. In addition to succeeding wherever the prior theory was successful, your attempt at a revolutionary theory must succeed here, too. Step 3: Your new theory must make new, testable predictions that differ from those of the original theory . Not only must you explain everything the old theory could, plus aspects of reality that the old theory couldn’t, but you must then show where new, yet-unmeasured predictions of your new theory and the old one differ, and then go out and measure the critical phenomena. Unless and until you clear all three of these steps, any claims of a scientific revolution are premature. A mural of the Einstein field equations, with an illustration of light bending around the eclipsed Sun: the key observations that first validated general relativity four years after it was first theoretically put forth: back in 1919. The Einstein tensor is shown decomposed, at left, into the Ricci tensor and Ricci scalar, with the cosmological constant term added in after that. If that constant weren’t included, an expanding (or collapsing) Universe would have been an inevitable consequence. Credit : Vysotsky / Wikimedia Commons Einstein’s general relativity only supplanted Newtonian gravity because it reproduced all of Newton’s successes, explained the advance of Mercury’s orbit in a way that Newton’s theory couldn’t, and then went beyond: predicting the deflection of starlight near the Sun during a total solar eclipse, which was only validated years later. Darwinian evolution by natural selection explains a great deal of what we observe, but the mechanism of inheritance — genetics, which itself was a foundational building block that led to the discovery of DNA and RNA: the underlying genetic code — would go far beyond anything Darwin could have anticipated. Nearly all of the novel ideas you hear about in science news will never even make it to “step 1” of this three-step formula; that’s how robust and well-established our current scientific ideas are across most fields. Most of the ideas that you read about in the popular press cannot even reproduce the full suite of successes of the currently accepted scientific picture; the ideas are that well-established, and concocting a viable alternative is more difficult than most people recognize. When someone says “it’s just a theory” about one of the well-established scientific theories that fall into this category (and yes, this category includes the science of human-caused climate change and global warming), remind them of the important difference between an unsubstantiated idea, guess, or hypothesis, and a robust scientific theory. Although nearly all of our theories are almost certainly not the final, ultimate answer, they are the best, most successful way we have to make sense of the Universe we inhabit. Equating those successes with someone’s uneducated guess is an insult to the very enterprise of human civilization. Yearly surface temperature compared to the 20th-century average from 1880–2021. Blue bars indicate cooler-than-average years; red bars show warmer-than-average years. Not included in this analysis is data from 2023, which has been recently confirmed as the hottest year yet on record. The warming, on average, is by 0.07 C per decade, but has accelerated in recent years, warming at an average of 0.18 C per decade since 1981. Credit : NOAA National Centers for Environmental information, Climate at a Glance: Global Time Series But what about “string theory” and other “theories” like that? Sometimes, people will bring up examples of theories that scientists study, but that are still only speculative as far as the evidence is concerned, in an attempt to undermine the successes of established scientific theory. What about: string theory, grand unified theory, the theory of extra dimensions, or some other idea or hypothesis that has the word “theory” in its name, but that doesn’t rise to the same standards of evidence as our established scientific theories? There are two good reasons for that type of name, however. One of them comes from science: they are theories in the stage of “theory development,” awaiting testing and confirmation that may or may not bear them out. The other is a different definition of theory: one that comes from mathematics . In mathematics, a theory doesn’t need to reflect reality, but rather occurs where you start with a set of axioms — mathematical rules for your system — and those axioms provide you with a framework to derive the properties of any element within that system. Mathematical theories are often the foundational starting point for what will lead to physical theories, and the sandbox of ideas that theoretical physicists most frequently play in is usually based on mathematical extensions to our presently known, accepted physical theories. A physical and mathematical theory can be related, but there is a distinction between how scientists and mathematicians use the word itself. This important difference explains why, although both string theory and quantum field theory have “theory” in their name, only quantum field theory is established, validated science. String theory, although it is a robust mathematical theory, remains in the realm of “speculative” on scientific grounds. This particle chart shows the pattern of charges W (weak isospin), W’ (weaker isospin), g3 and g8 (strong force charges), and B (baryon minus lepton number) within the SO(10) grand unified theory. The pattern has been rotated to show its embedding within the larger E6 group: the group that is expected to arise when string theory scenarios break down (or compactify) from 10 (or 11) to four spacetime dimensions. Credit : Cjean42/Wikimedia Commons Unless your theory has that predictive, explanatory power that has proven itself successful time and time again, over a wide variety of physical tests, there’s a very good chance that the “theory” you’re talking about is a theory only in the colloquial sense of the word. Without clearing all of those necessary hurdles, it isn’t a bona fide, accepted, valid scientific theory. String theory is a theory in the mathematical sense, but until its predictions become testable and are validated by those tests, it cannot be taken to be a definitive description of reality. Same for grand unified theories, theories of extra dimensions, the theory of supersymmetry, and many others. They may yet turn out to be true, but science demands that the evidence supports their validity before we can accept any of them. So yes, your Uncle Randy’s theory about the lizard people, your brother-in-law Fred’s theory about the Loch Ness monster, and Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity can all be called theories in our everyday language, but only one of them is an accepted theory in the scientific sense. Randy and Fred have theories that are merely speculative and unsubstantiated ideas, whereas Albert’s theory represents the pinnacle of modern scientific knowledge. The next time someone tells you that Einstein’s relativity is “just a theory,” you’ll be able to fully appreciate precisely how powerful, and important, being a scientific theory truly is! doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02136-5.title: Regional land carbon shifts strengthen atmospheric carbon dioxide–land carbon flux coupling
doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02136-5.summary: Nature Geoscience, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02136-5 Changes in the regional contribution to the flux of carbon from land have become more coupled to interannual atmospheric carbon dioxide fluctuations from 1959 to 2022, making land carbon sink variability more detectable, according to models and observations.

doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02142-7.title: Elevated early Eocene atmospheric CO 2 tied to reduced Southern Ocean biological pump efficiency
doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02142-7.summary: Abstract The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum (53 to 49 million years ago) was an interval in Earth’s history when reconstructed temperatures and atmospheric CO 2 concentrations were among the highest of the Cenozoic Era (that is, the last 66 million years). The causes of the high CO 2 levels remain unclear. CO 2 changes over recent ice age cycles appear to be largely controlled by the biologically mediated build-up and release of carbon from the Southern Ocean, a process that might have also played a role earlier in the Cenozoic. Here we test this possibility with foraminifera-bound nitrogen isotope measurements. Our data show higher surface nitrate concentrations in the Southern Ocean, and thus a more inefficient biological sequestration of carbon during peak Early Eocene Climatic Optimum. The associated transfer of CO 2 from the deep ocean to the atmosphere would have been amplified by the low seawater buffering capacity of the Eocene, due to the lower pH and high Ca ion concentration. Previously proposed low silicate rock weatherability during the Eocene may have weakened the weathering thermostat, allowing the reconstructed change in biological pump efficiency in the Southern Ocean to explain at least half of the atmospheric CO 2 increase observed during the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum.

doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02795-7.title: Declining environmental predictability erodes reproduction in a tropical seabird
doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02795-7.summary: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 13 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02795-7 The authors show that, for a tropical seabird model species, winter–spring phytoplankton blooms kept a stable mean timing but became more variable between years. Breeding synchrony weakened and reproductive success declined and became less consistent over the same two decades.

doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02769-9.title: Coal power lives longer next to data centres
doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02769-9.summary: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02769-9 Data centres are among the world’s fastest growing electricity consumers. An analysis of more than 9,000 facilities worldwide links the artificial intelligence-era expansion of data centres to delayed coal plant retirements and around 2 Gt of additional carbon dioxide emissions.

doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02789-5.title: Higher warming leads to a larger zero-emissions commitment
doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02789-5.summary: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02789-5 Scientific grounds for a net-zero policy assume near-zero committed warming over a few decades after CO2 emissions cease. A modelling study suggests that if prior peak temperatures rise above 2 °C before cessation of CO2 emissions, committed warming increases, making it harder to stabilize global warming.

doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02821-8.title: A further acceleration of clean energy is needed for global CO 2 emissions to peak and decline
doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02821-8.summary: Abstract Global fossil fuel CO 2 emissions have grown 0.8% per year on average between 2019 and 2025. Here we project a decrease of 0.4% in 2026, probably as a short-term response to the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict. Electric vehicles and solar and wind power offset about 64–79% of increasing emissions from demand growth through 2028; acceleration in clean technology deployment is needed to guarantee emissions peak and subsequent decline.

doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02794-8.title: Early evidence links data centre exposure to coal power retirement timelines
doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02794-8.summary: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02794-8 Data centre expansion may slow the coal-fired power plants phase-out, complicating decarbonization pathways. This study finds that coal units exposed to post-2020 data centres have lower retirement risks and their potential lifetime extensions could cause large additional CO2 emissions.

doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02797-5.title: Regional climate change approaches Paris limits
doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02797-5.summary: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02797-5 It has been surprisingly difficult to calculate how much warming different regions of the Earth have experienced since pre-industrial times. Now, research shows that in most land regions, the temperature thresholds that governments agreed to in Paris to keep below are already dangerously close.

doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02790-y.title: All IPCC AR6 regions are close to their 1.5 °C- and 2 °C-equivalent warming limits
doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02790-y.summary: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02790-y Climate targets are set for global temperatures, but what they mean regionally is less clear. Here the authors quantify the amount of human-induced warming in individual IPCC regions and find that, by 2025, they had reached 90–94% (65–76%) of their expected warming levels at the 1.5 °C (2 °C) global warming thresholds.

doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02786-8.title: Managing risk in carbon portfolios
doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02786-8.summary: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02786-8 Carbon removal methodologies have different risks of stored CO2 leaking back to the atmosphere. Now a study provides a quantitative framework for comparison, a necessary tool for building carbon storage portfolios with improved delivery, valuation and cost.

doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79569-4.title: Emergent mesoscale nanoparticle patterns from a non-equilibrium liquid lens
doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79569-4.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 14 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79569-4 Nanoparticle assembly at fluid interfaces is often viewed as unpredictable and dominated by uncontrolled non-equilibrium effects. Here, the authors show that evaporation-driven nanoparticle assembly reveals predictable morphologies through multiscale modeling, linking transport dynamics and kinetic arrest.

doi:10.1038/s41612-026-01590-7.title: Spatially adaptive neighboring information improves constraints on local temperature projections
doi:10.1038/s41612-026-01590-7.summary: Abstract Adaptation needs local temperature projections, yet their uncertainty remains large. Historical temperature differences between observations and the model-ensemble mean contain unforced variability, substantially limiting constraints on future local warming. Whether neighboring records strengthen these constraints, and at what spatial scale, remains a key unresolved question. We show that distance-weighted averaging of observation–model differences within a fixed radius improves skill over using only the target-grid record. This improvement arises because nearby locations share forced warming signals, allowing averaging to reduce noise while retaining information about future warming at the target. We therefore develop an adaptive observational constraint that selects the neighborhood radius and weights neighboring information according to its noise and relevance to target warming. It improves skill over the target-grid constraint in 33 of 34 SSP5-8.5 models at a 50-year lead and in both lower-forcing SSPs. Applied to HadCRUT5, it lowers projected late-century local warming under SSP5-8.5 and narrows spread.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2607859123.title: On-site, subannual climate records decouple Neolithic expansion from climate instability
doi:10.1073/pnas.2607859123.summary: How the life of prehistoric people was influenced by climate change and extreme events often remains elusive. Finding appropriate spatiotemporal scales is the major challenge for studies with socioenvironmental questions. This challenge can be overcome by sourcing climatic information from archaeological sites, alongside traces of human agency. For instance, extreme cold-events have been proposed as causing a standstill in early farming expansion across the Mediterranean 8600-8000 years ago. However, there is no immediate (local/short-term) evidence of such events and how they might have influenced people’s lives, nor have previous records been sufficiently resolved to test this robustly. Here we statistically assess the influence of on-site and short-term extremes on human decision-making hypothesized by long-term climate records. Using the largest dataset yet of high-resolution temperature archives in mollusks, we test whether early farmers would have been exposed to extreme cold-events, compromising their subsistence by reducing harvest yields. This immediate agricultural risk is argued to have prevented the spread of new settlements and thus delayed the vigorous expansion that followed, one of prehistory’s fastest known dispersals. Direct comparison of paleotemperature and subsistence data from the same archaeological contexts shows no winter cooling of the magnitude proposed for this period, and no strong relationship between climate and subsistence. Our study reveals how a major scale mismatch in climate-society research can be resolved at the site level, integrating climatic variability on the subannual timescale crucial to farming, and provides a direct, local empirical test of a long-assumed climate impact.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2533000123.title: Environmental forcing, individual repeatability, and mother–daughter resemblance shape the phenology of a long-lived seabird
doi:10.1073/pnas.2533000123.summary: Climate change and variability push species to shift their distributions and phenology to track their climatic niche. Predicting population responses requires identifying the environmental cues that trigger reproduction, their fitness consequences, and the intrinsic factors that shape individual breeding decisions. In long-lived species with deferred breeding, extrinsic (environmental) and intrinsic (individual/maternal) factors may interact in shaping responses to environmental change, but direct empirical evidence remains scarce. We use 2065 breeding events collected over 22 y on a wide-ranging seabird, the Scopoli’s Shearwater. We quantify the effects on population mean laying date of a large-scale climatic index (wNAO) associated with oceanographic conditions. We assess how individual breeding experience and mother–daughter resemblance contribute to among-female differences in reproductive timing, and evaluate the consequences for breeding success (BS) and adult survival. Average laying date was earlier under negative phases of wNAO, indicating a plastic response at the population level. Individual repeatability in the relative laying date (RLD) was high ( R = 0.50) irrespective of experience, indicating consistency among females. Using 142 mother–daughter cases, daughters’ RLD resembled those of their mothers, a covariance that may reflect genetic inheritance, maternal effects, or shared environment. Early laying was associated with higher BS and survival, translating into an annual fitness advantage. Differences in survival and BS across individuals were more evident during the first observed breeding attempts. Together, these results support a scenario in which plasticity shifts the population mean breeding date in response to climatic variation, while persistent traits generate differential fitness among individuals.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2621335123.title: Geochemical signatures of magnetite are conserved in diverse populations of environmental magnetotactic bacteria
doi:10.1073/pnas.2621335123.summary: Magnetotactic bacteria (MTB) synthesize intracellular magnetite nanoparticles in a genetically controlled manner. They may represent some of the earliest biomineralizing organisms on Earth, and a unique window into ancient life and the environments that hosted it. Yet, identification of their mineralogical remains in ancient rocks is highly challenging due to the lack of reliable and lasting proxies. Previous results obtained from laboratory cultures of single strains of MTB revealed trace element and Fe isotope patterns that are not shared by any other source of magnetite, which could be used as reliable proxies for the identification of ancient MTB. However, the environmental relevance of these previous findings for environmental and mixed population of MTB is unknown. We report the trace element and Fe isotope compositions of magnetite extracted from environmental MTB collected in the water column of Lake Pavin, France, and show that the most distinctive geochemical traits (enrichment in Mo, Se, Sn, and light Fe isotopes) of magnetite produced by MTB cultivated in the laboratory are conserved in environmental populations. They represent potential biological signatures that can be searched in ancient rocks and coupled with magnetic and mineralogical tracers to support the presence of MTB and reconstruct their emergence and evolution.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2611210123.title: Forcing dataset updates impact regional but not global Earth radiation budget trends in the GFDL AM4 climate model
doi:10.1073/pnas.2611210123.summary: The availability of up-to-date forcing datasets is critical for reconciling Earth system model simulations with contemporary observations. With the newly released CMIP7 forcing dataset, which extends the historical record through 2021, this study provides a systematic evaluation of how using updated forcings over the “middle-of-the-road” SSP2-4.5 scenario forcings influences the simulated radiation budget in the GFDL AM4 climate model. The updated forcing dataset used in the atmosphere model does not improve the agreement between the simulated global-mean top-of-the-atmosphere radiation trends and the satellite-observed trends. Regionally, we identify pronounced shifts in radiative energy partitioning between atmosphere and surface. Specifically, during 2001–2021, accelerated reductions in sulfate and black carbon aerosols over East Asia drive a significant decline in atmospheric solar absorption that matches observations, while a substantial increase in organic aerosols at higher latitudes induces a localized increase in atmospheric absorption that does not match observations. The substantial influence of localized forcing changes on simulated regional climate underscores the necessity for routine updates of forcing datasets.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2613542123.title: Coupling of structural preordering and density fluctuation: A unified picture of nucleation in metallic glasses
doi:10.1073/pnas.2613542123.summary: Crystallization is ubiquitous in nature and technology, occurring in pharmaceuticals, biomacromolecules, polymers, metallurgy and glass formation. Yet how crystallization proceeds, particularly at its earliest stage, remains elusive. Studies on glass-forming liquids increasingly suggest that crystallization initiates in structurally preordered regions, with density fluctuations playing a secondary role, a view widely generalized from hard-sphere colloids. Here we show, across disordered metallic systems from pure elements and intermetallic compounds to glass-forming alloys, that density fluctuations and structural preordering emerge simultaneously during nucleation. This coupling reflects local atomic rearrangements in which free-volume reduction, denser packing, and bond-orientational order develop together. Our findings provide a physical basis for a unified nucleation framework for disordered materials.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2623623123.title: Afforestation reshapes wildfire activity across global temperate biomes
doi:10.1073/pnas.2623623123.summary: In temperate ecosystems, afforestation is rapidly expanding as a flagship climate mitigation strategy. Yet its impact on wildfires remains poorly understood, raising concerns that establishing planted forests over nonforest areas may intensify wildfire activity under increasingly fire-prone climatic conditions. Here, we combine land-use change data, fire activity records, climatic and anthropogenic covariates to quantify how afforestation alters fire occurrence and burned area across 67,248 patches distributed throughout global temperate biomes using satellite records starting in 2001. We found that, on average, afforestation increased fire occurrence by 26% and burned area by 23% in global temperate regions. However, these effects differed markedly among biomes. Wildfire responses ranged from a near-threefold increase in fire occurrence in Temperate Conifer Forests and a 38% increase in Mediterranean Woodlands biomes to an 18% reduction in the Temperate Grasslands, Savannas, and Shrublands biome. In Temperate Broadleaf and Mixed Forests, afforestation reduced fire occurrence but increased burned area, indicating a shift toward less frequent but larger wildfires following the conversion to planted forest. These contrasting, biome-specific responses show that the consequences of afforestation on wildfire activity may depend strongly on ecological and regional context. The strong variability at biome-scale questions the premise that tree planting provides consistent climate mitigation benefits across all landscapes, and highlights the need to evaluate afforestation initiatives alongside regional disturbance regimes. Our findings indicate that wildfire risk should be explicitly accounted for when assessing the long-term effectiveness of afforestation as a climate mitigation strategy in a warming world.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2616833123.title: Municipal sludge disposal emerges as a major, hidden, and rapidly growing atmospheric mercury source
doi:10.1073/pnas.2616833123.summary: Wastewater treatment greatly reduces mercury pollution in aquatic ecosystems but does not eliminate it. Here, we identify municipal sludge disposal as a major, long-overlooked atmospheric mercury source. In China, sludge disposal emitted 42 - 10 + 18 Mg in 2024, exceeding 10% of national anthropogenic emissions and ranking third after cement production and nonferrous metal smelting. These emissions have increased by nearly a thousandfold since the 1970s and are concentrated in densely populated urban areas, driven by the rapid expansion of sludge incineration, codisposal, and composting. Our findings reveal a cross-media pollution transfer embedded in sustainability transitions and call for sludge disposal to be incorporated into UNEP mercury budget and Minamata Convention assessments.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2636808123.title: Correction for Fahy et al., Hydroxyl radical oxidation of chemical contaminants on indoor surfaces and dust
doi:10.1073/pnas.2636808123.summary: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 45, November 2026.

doi:10.1126/science.aed9544.title: Atmospheric O2 reveals a strengthening ocean carbon sink and a stagnant net land sink since 1990
doi:10.1126/science.aed9544.summary: The global ocean and land biosphere absorb roughly half of fossil fuel carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions. The temporal evolution of these sinks remains difficult to quantify owing to data sparsity. Leveraging 30+ years of atmospheric oxygen (O 2 ) and CO 2 observations, we find that the ocean carbon sink increased by 0.63 ± 0.19 petagrams of carbon per year per decade (Pg C year −1 decade −1 ) (a mean of 2.8 ± 0.4 Pg C year −1 ), accounting for 35% of fossil emissions between 1990 and 2019. The net land sink shows no robust trend (with a mean of 1.0 ± 0.5 Pg C year −1 , accounting for 13% of fossil emissions), despite large decadal variability. These results challenge many process-based model simulations of the land and ocean sinks, questioning their ability to accurately predict future climate states.

doi:10.1126/science.aeg2366.title: Climate aridity amplifies global riverine nitrate beyond human inputs
doi:10.1126/science.aeg2366.summary: Nitrate pollution is widely perceived as a signature of human inputs. Here we show, with machine-learning reconstructed global maps, that climate aridity is also a dominant driver, systematically elevating nitrate concentrations across land-use gradients and creating unexpected hotspots beyond major agricultural and urban centers. Across ~2.9 million river segments worldwide, nitrate concentrations exceed ecological and health thresholds across ~33 and 2% of global land area, affecting ~5.6 billion (73%) and 0.5 billion (6%) people, respectively. Ecological threshold exceedance occurs mostly in headwaters, and about half of the health threshold exceedance occurs in middle-income countries and sparsely populated landscapes. These findings cast nitrate pollution as an aridity-amplified risk, suggesting that aridification may increase nitrate exposure even without additional human inputs. They call for regulatory standards that reflect risks across broad concentration ranges.

doi:10.1126/science.adw7770.title: Carbon dioxide and amorphous water ices in the debris disk around β Pictoris
doi:10.1126/science.adw7770.summary: The star β Pictoris is orbited by a dusty debris disk, within which planet formation is occurring. The outer disk is sufficiently far from the star that volatile molecules are expected to freeze into solid ices. We observed the β Pictoris disk in the near-infrared using the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectrum shows features due to amorphous water ice (<7% crystallinity) and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) ice in both the 12 CO 2 and 13 CO 2 isotopologues. We infer that the CO 2 ice is intimately mixed with the water ice at a ratio of 1:10. This implies that the ices formed in cold conditions, likely in the interstellar medium. Frequent collisions within the debris disk are required to explain the observed uniform distribution of icy dust grains.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeg9077.title: Brown carbon in biomass burning aerosol enhances HONO production
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeg9077.summary: Nitrous acid (HONO) is an important source of hydroxyl radicals (•OH). •OH drives ozone and aerosol formation, affecting air quality, health, and climate. Elevated HONO concentrations have been observed in biomass burning (BB) plumes. However, the mechanism remains unclear, hindering parameterization and quantification of the impacts. Here, we conducted flow tube experiments with BB aerosol samples and proxies to investigate renoxification, a process that converts nitrate into HONO and NO x (NO and NO 2 ). Our results reveal that renoxification in BB aerosol is enhanced by brown carbon (BrC) through electron transfer to nitrate as an alternative to surface-enhanced nitrate photolysis. We develop parameterization to assess the potential global impacts of BrC-enhanced renoxification, which suggests that BrC enhances surface-level HONO production by up to one order of magnitude in BB-affected regions, with surface HONO production exceeding 1 part per trillion per hour in regions with high aerosol nitrate. These impacts are expected to worsen as BB intensifies in a warming climate.
