doi:10.5194/acp-26-16101-2026.title: Characterization of trace gas emissions from controlled laboratory burning of Canadian boreal forest fuels
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16101-2026.summary: Although boreal wildfires are a major global source of trace gases, their emissions remain poorly characterized. To address this gap, controlled burns of Canadian Boreal surface and ground fuels were conducted during the Biomass Burning Canada (BBCan) Campaign. Emission factors (EF) for 46 volatile organic compounds (VOC) were determined using iodide chemical ionization mass spectrometry (I-CIMS) and Vocus proton transfer reaction mass spectrometry (Vocus PTR-MS). Total non-methane organic compound (NMOC) emissions, which were measured separately, were found to account for 2 %–12 % of total emitted gas-phase carbon (i.e., CO 2 , CO, CH 4 , NMOC), with total quantified VOCs (∑VOCs) accounting for 13 %–40 % of that fraction. The dominant compounds contributing to the measured ∑VOCs include oxygenates and organic reactive nitrogen (Nr) species. Boreal peat fuels, which are prone to residual smoldering combustion, produced significantly higher total NMOC, total Nr, and individual VOC emissions than the other fuels. In contrast, boreal mulch, which burned very efficiently, produced low emissions. Combustion efficiency was observed to have a strong impact on total and individual VOC emissions, but VOC emission profiles were also dependent on fuel type and moisture content. The findings indicate that the EFs currently used to speciate NMOC emission may not adequately capture emissions from smoldering boreal peat fires. Study results provide the first comprehensive VOC EF for fresh emissions for a range of Canadian boreal surface and ground fuels, which can be used to improve emission inventories and enhance predictions of wildfire smoke impacts on air quality, climate, and health.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16067-2026.title: Process-level contributions to uncertainty in aerosol effective radiative forcing: a perturbed parameter ensemble with ICON–HAM
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16067-2026.summary: Changes in aerosols since the preindustrial era have altered the top-of-the-atmosphere radiation balance by scattering and absorbing solar radiation (aerosol–radiation interactions, ARI) and indirectly interacting with clouds (aerosol–cloud interactions, ACI), known as aerosol effective radiative forcing (ERF aer ). ERF aer persistently remains one of the most uncertain components in climate projections, due to imperfect representations of aerosol and cloud processes in climate models. Here, we construct a perturbed parameter ensemble (PPE) with the aerosol–climate model ICON2.6.4–A–HAM2.3 (hereafter ICON–HAM) to quantify key sources of ERF aer uncertainty. We perturb 42 aerosol and cloud parameters over 383 PPE members. Parametric uncertainties in aerosol and cloud processes yield a 90 % credible range of −1.42 to −0.65 W m −2 for ERF aer (mean: −1.04 W m −2 ) for the period 2024–2025. The parameters related to emissions (anthropogenic sulfur dioxide, natural dimethyl sulfide, and emitted particle size) dominate ACI uncertainty and hence ERF aer uncertainty (80 %), while absorption-related parameters (anthropogenic black carbon emissions and aerosol refractive indices) drive ARI uncertainty (60 %). Cloud parameters account for 13 % of ERF aer uncertainty, mainly via convection and entrainment processes. The sensitivity analysis of model diagnostics to parameters reveals that many present-day aerosol and cloud observables share dominant causes of uncertainty with ACI and ARI forcing, highlighting the potential for constraining ERF aer using existing space- and ground-based measurements. Notably, model biases against SPEXone and MODIS observations coincide spatially with parametric uncertainties, suggesting that much of these biases may be mitigated through appropriate constraint with observations, while the remainder requires structural model developments in combination with improved observations.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-15975-2026.title: Evaluation and improvement of the cold pool parameterization in the LMDZ climate model against Large Eddy Simulations
doi:10.5194/acp-26-15975-2026.summary: Cold pools, formed under clouds by the evaporation of precipitation, play a central role in maintaining and organizing atmospheric convection. It is suspected that their absence in climate models may lead to significant errors in the representation of convection, such as the premature convection extinction after sunset. The introduction of a cold pool parameterization into the LMDZ climate model has significantly improved the representation of convection, in particular its diurnal cycle. Thanks to this indirect evaluation, the parameterization of cold pool was retained in the further versions of LMDZ. However, no evaluation of the representations of cold pools themselves was done so far. This work provides for the first time such an evaluation based on Large Eddy Simulation (LES). The evaluation is done both on a case of radiative–convective equilibrium that allows the study of convective processes in a well-controlled and quasi-stationary framework, without the influence of large-scale dynamics, and on the time-dependent continental case AMMA (African Monsoon Multidisciplinary Analysis), representative of typical Sahelian conditions with local initiation during the afternoon. First, we evaluate the physical relationships underlying the cold pool model in the LES, then, in a second step, its behavior when coupled with the deep convection scheme in the single-column version of LMDZ. The analyses carried out demonstrate the relevance of the assumptions underlying the parameterization. The initial version actually captures the main characteristics of LES cold pools but also exhibits some biases. We show how substantial modifications to the cold pool scheme and a readjustment of certain free parameters helped reduce those biases significantly. The remaining flaws could be corrected by adding convective mixing through thermal plumes within the cold pools and by modeling the evolution of cold pools number density rather than imposing it.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16047-2026.title: Frequent occurrence of newly formed aerosol particles over wide geographical areas in the Arctic free troposphere and atmospheric boundary layer
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16047-2026.summary: New particle formation (NPF) can impact the Arctic radiative energy budget since this region is particularly sensitive to changes in aerosol particle and cloud condensation nuclei concentrations. Prior measurements have predominantly investigated NPF in the Arctic atmospheric boundary layer (ABL), while vertically-resolved studies on newly formed aerosol particles remain scarce. Here, we present an analysis which suggests that NPF may take place throughout the entire lower Arctic troposphere. We have reached this conclusion by analyzing aerosol particle number size distribution data collected during a springtime aircraft campaign (BACSAM II) in the vicinity of Svalbard, the Fram Strait, and northern Greenland. We detected newly formed aerosol particles over distances of hundreds of kilometers, at various altitudes ranging from about 60 to 3900 m, and identified four atmospheric scenarios for their occurrence: newly formed particles in the free troposphere, in the ABL over sea ice, in the vicinity of clouds, and in the ABL over ocean with sea ice floes. Our results indicate that regional Arctic atmospheric processes as well as long-range transport may play key roles in the formation of new particles. In particular, we deduce that one possible mechanism leading to free tropospheric NPF could be associated with warm-air intrusions.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16013-2026.title: Methane in the Asian Monsoon anticyclone and global UTLS behavior observed in ACE-FTS satellite data
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16013-2026.summary: Methane in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS) plays a critical role in atmospheric composition and radiative forcing, yet the processes governing its vertical structure and variability remain poorly understood. Here, we use high-quality satellite observations from the Atmospheric Chemistry Experiment Fourier Transform Spectrometer (ACE-FTS) to characterize the vertical structure and global seasonal behavior of methane in the UTLS, with emphasis on the role of Asian Summer Monsoon (ASM). In the ASM, a maximum in methane concentration occurs near the tropopause, at a higher altitude than the corresponding carbon monoxide maximum. The largest relative enhancement for methane – the difference between air inside and outside the anticyclone – occurs above the tropopause and extends poleward to the north. This behavior contrasts with carbon monoxide, which is confined within the anticyclone. The seasonal cycle of methane near the tropical tropopause peaks in boreal autumn, following the summer peak in surface fluxes and deep convection. This phase lag reflects the combined effects of ASM transport and subsequent large-scale redistribution following the breakdown of the anticyclone. Positive anomalies occur in the tropical lower stratosphere in boreal winter, consistent with the upwelling branch of the Brewer–Dobson circulation (BDC). Beyond the seasonal cycle, ACE-FTS data show a pronounced hemispheric asymmetry in lower stratospheric methane trends, consistent with reported changes in other long-lived trace constituents. Together, these results provide new observational evidence that ASM transport imprints a distinct methane structure above the tropopause and plays a key role in shaping UTLS variability on a global scale.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16029-2026.title: Evaluating the representativeness of aircraft sampling strategies for cloud water content in LASSO simulations over the ARM Southern Great Plains (SGP) Site
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16029-2026.summary: Aircraft observations are widely used to evaluate cloud simulations; however, their inherently localized sampling may not fully represent the domain-scale cloud properties resolved by large-eddy simulations (LES). This study quantifies how aircraft-like sampling strategies influence the representativeness of in-cloud cloud water content (CWC) derived from LES output. Using LASSO simulations for the ARM Southern Great Plains site (SGP), we emulate aircraft trajectories by prescribing multiple horizontal flight patterns (circle, diagonal, straight, combo, and zigzag) and vertical profiles (level-leg, sine wave, staircase, and zigzag) under different speed categories. Results show that sampling geometry substantially influences the degree to which aircraft-like measurements capture the magnitude and variability of domain-scale CWC. Sampling representativeness depends jointly on flight speed and trajectory geometry. For the level-leg, sine wave, and staircase vertical profiles, increasing flight speed generally improves agreement with the layer-restricted in-cloud domain mean by increasing spatial coverage and reducing sensitivity to localized heterogeneity. In contrast, the zigzag pattern does not show systematic improvement with speed because its phase-locked vertical–horizontal coupling constrains effective spatial coverage. Cloud-boundary analysis further indicates the tendency to underestimate cloud-top height, while cloud-base height is more consistently captured, with higher speeds reducing both bias and variability. These findings establish a systematic framework for interpreting aircraft-based cloud measurements in the context of LES output and highlight the importance of sampling strategies in assessing representativeness in model–observation comparisons.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16003-2026.title: New particle formation contribution to aerosol mass: regimes and implications for future urban environments
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16003-2026.summary: New particle formation (NPF) is a major source of global aerosol number concentration yet its contribution to aerosol mass remains unclear. Here we propose a regime framework for NPF mass contributions using aerosol dynamic simulations constrained by atmospheric measurements. We show that new particles can contribute more than 10 µg m −3 to particle mass under conditions characterized by high initial new particle concentrations, high condensable vapor production rates, and low background condensation sink (CS bg ). Among these influencing factors, the initial CS bg governs NPF mass contribution under the simulation conditions: NPF contributes significantly to aerosol surface area and mass at an initial CS bg of ∼ 0.001 s −1 (regime I), while its contribution becomes negligible when CS bg exceeds 0.01 s −1 (regime III). Results show that NPF events in urban Beijing occur mostly in a transition regime (initial CS bg 0.001–0.01 s −1 , regime II), in which the NPF mass contribution is also modulated by the mass accommodation coefficient of background particles, while events at a Finnish forest site fall in regimes I and II. Our simulations suggest that NPF mass contribution in urban environments with a declining CS bg will shift toward regimes I and II. This indicates that control of anthropogenic NPF precursors may represent an effective strategy for present and future particulate matter pollution in urban environments, which warrants further investigation.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-15877-2026.title: Impact of aerosol absorption and scattering on winter fog lifecycle: insights from NWP simulations over Indo-Gangetic Plains
doi:10.5194/acp-26-15877-2026.summary: The Indo-Gangetic Plains (IGP) of India frequently experience widespread and dense winter fog with substantial health and economic consequences. This season also coincides with elevated aerosol loading. This study investigates the influence of aerosols on the development and evolution of dense fog over the IGP using high-resolution numerical experiments. We focus especially on the relative contributions of absorption and scattering to aerosol-radiation interactions (ARI). While aerosol-cloud interactions related to fog have been extensively studied, the role of ARI has received relatively less attention, due to the limited prevalence of absorbing aerosols in many other parts of the world. However, the increasing number of absorbing aerosols over IGP prompted this study to isolate and examine the contributions of both scattering and absorbing components of ARI. Satellite-derived absorbing aerosol indices confirmed the presence of absorbing aerosols over the study region. The results of numerical experiments reveal that disabling the aerosol absorption component of ARI nearly doubled the area affected by dense fog, increased fog height by more than 20 %, and delayed fog dissipation by about 2 h. In contrast, turning off the scattering component of ARI reduced fog coverage by 18 %. Scattering effects were spatially uniform, promoting the vertical growth of fog. Conversely, absorption had a spatially variable impact, enhancing or suppressing fog height depending on whether the absorbing aerosols resided within or above the boundary layer. These findings emphasise the need to accurately represent ARI in numerical weather prediction models for improved fog forecasting over aerosol-rich regions like the IGP.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-15953-2026.title: Technical note: Integrating generative AI with physics-based simulations for probabilistic modelling of volcanic clouds
doi:10.5194/acp-26-15953-2026.summary: Ensemble-based modelling of the atmospheric dispersal of volcanic clouds enables more realistic forecasts by explicitly accounting for uncertainties in eruption source parameters, meteorological data, and systematic errors in transport models. Many ensemble applications, including forecast uncertainty quantification, data assimilation, and probabilistic hazard assessment, require large ensembles to reduce sampling errors and adequately represent probability distributions. However, simulating and processing large ensembles with atmospheric dispersal models can be computationally demanding, even on high-performance computing clusters. Generative AI offers a complementary approach by representing simulated fields in a lower-dimensional latent space, enabling new samples to be generated at low computational cost and facilitating the manipulation of large ensembles. A Variational AutoEncoder (VAE) is trained on ensembles of physics-based simulations and used to generate new samples. The learned latent-space representation is then used to test two ensemble-based data assimilation methods, demonstrating the potential benefits of performing data assimilation in a lower-dimensional space. As a proof of concept, the data assimilation problem is formulated in two dimensions. Two numerical experiments demonstrate that VAE-generated ensembles can reproduce key statistics of a larger reference ensemble and improve agreement with satellite retrievals. The VAE achieves up to a 1000-fold compression of the original fields into 16- and 32-dimensional latent spaces. The VAE-generated ensemble of 4096 members reduces RMSE by 4 % relative to the model prior, while latent-space data assimilation further reduces RMSE by 30 %. These results highlight the potential of generative AI to efficiently augment physics-based ensembles and improve forecasting skill through latent-space data assimilation.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-15915-2026.title: Probabilities of detection of methane plumes by remote sensing and implications for inferred emissions distributions
doi:10.5194/acp-26-15915-2026.summary: Strategies for mitigating methane emissions rely on understanding the underlying drivers of methane emissions to the atmosphere. Observations of methane plumes emerging from point sources, combined with correct statistical interpretation, can provide key information. In this work, we examine a critical parameter, the probability of detection of a plume. For a given observing system, probability of detection is affected by the properties of the sensor, plume detection algorithm, observing conditions, and emission rate of the source. We parameterize relevant aspects of remotely sensed scenes containing plumes using a nondimensional observability parameter that predicts probability of detection. Our probability of detection model is trained using simulated plumes to capture natural variability in different meteorological conditions, and validated with data from controlled release experiments. We model probability of detection for two airborne imaging spectrometer systems, MethaneAIR and Insight M LeakSurveyor™, and one high resolution satellite system, MethaneSAT. Monte Carlo simulations of emissions distributions implied by data from the extensive 2023 MAIRX campaign of MethaneAIR demonstrate the importance of an accurate probability of detection model to analyze observations from systems with higher emission rate thresholds for detection, due to the heavy tailed emission rate distribution found in most North American oil and gas basins. Additionally, we find that the frequency of rare, high impact emission events drives high uncertainty in distributions of total emissions by emission rate.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-15895-2026.title: Sensitivity of marine cloud brightening over the Great Barrier Reef to spatial variability in aerosol forcing: a case study using a convection-permitting model
doi:10.5194/acp-26-15895-2026.summary: The Great Barrier Reef (GBR) is increasingly threatened by mass thermal coral bleaching events under climate change. Marine cloud brightening (MCB) has been proposed as a potential adaptation strategy to reduce thermal stress by enhancing cloud reflectivity through aerosol injection. This study evaluates the sensitivity of cloud–aerosol interactions to aerosol emission intensity and spatial configuration over the GBR using convection-permitting Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations. A control simulation representing a non- to weakly-precipitating shallow trade-cumulus regime is compared with three MCB sensitivity experiments: a densely distributed (20 km apart), moderate emission flux scenario (EXP20), a sparsely distributed (100 km spacing), high emission flux scenario (EXP100), and an intermediate configuration (EXP40). Results show that enhanced aerosol emissions substantially increase near-surface aerosol concentrations, with dispersion strongly governed by source spacing and prevailing trade winds. The EXP20 configuration produces more homogeneous and widespread aerosol enhancements, whereas EXP100 generates localized peaks that are rapidly removed, resulting in smaller domain-mean increases despite identical total emissions. Over a 24 h period, domain-averaged cloud droplet number concentration (CDNC), optical depth, and cloud albedo exhibit strong sensitivity to aerosol loading, while cloud water path (CWP) and cloud fraction show limited responses. These findings indicate a dominant Twomey effect in this cloud regime, with only weak evidence of the Albrecht effect. Nonlinear CWP responses are noted under varying conditions of mid-level humidity, wind shear, and lower-tropospheric stability. Overall, the results highlight the importance of aerosol source configuration and background atmospheric state in shaping MCB effectiveness over the GBR.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-15853-2026.title: Drivers of biogenic secondary organic aerosol from the past to the future
doi:10.5194/acp-26-15853-2026.summary: Biogenic secondary organic aerosol (SOA) makes up a substantial fraction of atmospheric fine particulate mass, with implications for climate and human health. However, its chemical formation processes remain poorly understood and are often oversimplified in 3D models. Recent studies have found that the peroxy radical (RO 2 ) isomerization and the RO 2 accretion reactions (RO 2 + RO 2 ) can lead to SOA formation. We expand the RO 2 chemical mechanism in the Community Earth System Model version 2 to include these two additional pathways for biogenic SOA formed through the OH oxidation of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Using this mechanism, we quantify the contribution of each RO 2 pathway to biogenic SOA formation and examine how these contributions evolve from the pre-industrial (PI) to present-day (PD) and future (F). We find that in PD conditions, RO 2 isomerization accounts for nearly half of monoterpene SOA, while the contribution from RO 2 + RO 2 pathways is minor. From PI to F, the RO 2 fate varies in response to atmospheric NO x levels and climate, but the contribution from RO 2 isomerization is consistently high for monoterpenes, underscoring the importance of representing this pathway in SOA parameterizations. Total biogenic SOA formed through OH oxidation decreases by 41 % from PI to PD and increases by 112 % from PD to F. This evolution from PI to F is largely driven by changes in biogenic VOC emissions, rather than shifts in chemistry or thermodynamic partitioning. Our results highlight the need to better constrain RO 2 pathways for SOA formation through laboratory studies and represent this RO 2 chemistry in SOA modeling.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-15831-2026.title: The synergy of morphology and mixing state on the absorption of coated black carbon soot
doi:10.5194/acp-26-15831-2026.summary: Black carbon (BC) strongly absorbs light and contributes to climate warming. Coating formation on fractal BC-containing soot is a ubiquitous atmospheric process that enhances its absorption, but the extent of this absorption enhancement ( E abs ) remains uncertain and difficult to represent in models. In this study, we use large simulation chamber experiments to investigate BC absorption and its modification by coating formation and ageing. Polydisperse fractal BC-containing soot was mixed with non-absorbing atmospherically-relevant secondary aerosols (sulfuric acid and α -pinene secondary organic aerosols). Varying reaction dynamics produced different coating rates and masses, mimicking atmospheric processing. The evolution of soot and coating properties was tracked for up to 20 h. The results of this study suggest a general positive correlation between E abs and coating amount on soot. However, they also experimentally demonstrate the strong effect of morphological modifications and mixing state heterogeneity on BC absorption, both depending on the reaction dynamics of coating formation and ageing of the coated soot. Combined variations in morphology and mixing state affect the magnitude of E abs and its further evolution, leading, depending on processing, to either an increase or decrease in absorption. The range of measured E abs resulting from soot processing cannot be reliably represented using a fixed E abs value or by a core-shell optical model, two approximations commonly used in climate models. These results support the need for new formalisms that would take into account both morphological and mixing state heterogeneity to improve model predictions of BC absorption and its role on the radiative budget.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-15931-2026.title: Measurement report: Size-resolved seasonal study of inorganic ions and isotopic carbon signatures of aerosol particles at the Wadden Sea
doi:10.5194/acp-26-15931-2026.summary: Measurements of aerosol size-resolved chemical composition and source contribution of carbonaceous aerosols provide a unique opportunity to characterize continental outflow over the sea. Studies at coastal sites usually show an interesting mix of continental and marine aerosol sources. However, few data exist on the size dependence of the aerosol chemical composition and isotopic source apportionment of organic carbon (OC). This study investigates differences in aerosol composition among size-dependent samples collected in different seasons and wind sectors. It also highlights isotope measurements as a tool to study sources and atmospheric processing of OC. Size-resolved measurements of inorganic ions, levoglucosan, and total carbon (TC) were combined with 13 C and 14 C analysis of OC at different desorption temperatures, which allows to investigate subgroups like secondary organic aerosol (SOA) and aged organic aerosol. The land-sector samples are dominated by nitrate, ammonium, and TC, while sulfate and TC dominated the single sea-sector sample set. Sulfate reached 0.5 µg m −3 in both sea-sector and land-sector samples, indicating a possible contribution from ship-emissions. Fossil OC fractions were highest in particles <250 nm, characteristic for combustion-related traffic emissions. 13C/12C-ratios of ambient OC deviate strongly from expected signatures of primary sources and indicate SOA contribution to more volatile carbon and smaller particles. The 13C/12C-ratios of less volatile OC at larger sizes are consistent with a significant influence of photochemical processing. The results indicate shipping emissions as a possible important contributor to sulfate aerosols in sea-influenced samples and demonstrate the highly processed nature of OC in the European continental outflow.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-15813-2026.title: Revisiting the parameterization of ice nucleation of dust particles under mixed-phase cloud conditions from laboratory measurements
doi:10.5194/acp-26-15813-2026.summary: Dust aerosol plays a key role in cloud formation and evolution due to its high atmospheric abundance and efficient ice nucleation ability (INA). A generalized parameterization of dust-induced ice formation in climate models remains challenging, because dust INA varies substantially with mineral composition, aerosol generation methods, and atmospheric aging processes. In this study, we revisited the INA of dust particles under mixed-phase cloud conditions (MPC, −38 < T < 0 °C) compiled from previous laboratory studies. Our results indicate that INA of dust particles with different mineral compositions exhibit variability spanning up to 6 orders of magnitude in INA at −38 < T < −2 °C. When accounting for mineralogical differences, aerosol generation methods whether particles are dry-dispersed or wet-suspended also contribute to the reported variability. This sample preparation difference likely arises from variations in water-particle interactions time scales that are longer in the suspension than the aerosol measurements. Aging generally reduces dust INA, with chemical reactions inducing the strongest reduction, followed by thermal treatments and water/aqueous aging. Based on these findings, we developed a suite of n s -based parameterizations to represent INA of dust particles with mixed and specific mineral composition. We also proposed parameterizations based on D e (spherical equivalent particle diameter within a droplet), which predict droplet freezing across the full MPC temperature range using a single expression. These empirical parameterizations capture the general INA trends of dust particles and are expected to improve the accuracy of predictions of dust-induced cloud formation in climate models.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-15757-2026.title: Correct use of radiative efficiencies in calculating global warming potentials and other emission metrics
doi:10.5194/acp-26-15757-2026.summary: The calculations of Global Warming Potentials (GWPs) and other related climate emission metrics should use radiative efficiencies that are calculated using the mean atmospheric mole fraction, rather than the surface mole fraction as is commonly used. We quantify this correction and show it leads to an upward revision of GWP values. For species with lifetimes greater than a few years, the revision is an increase of a few percent e.g., 7 % for trichlorofluoromethane (CFC-11). For species with lifetimes of the order of a year or less, this correction can lead to increases in the GWPs of over ten percent, which could impact on stakeholder decisions on the desirability of using such gases.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-15735-2026.title: CO emissions and NOx ∕ CO ratios from the extreme 2025 Iberian wildfires: TROPOMI-based estimates and comparison with inventories
doi:10.5194/acp-26-15735-2026.summary: In summer 2025 the Iberian Peninsula experienced exceptional wildfire activity, with nearly 0.5 Mha of land burned and carbon emissions that broke European records since 2003. In this work, we quantify CO emission rates from 15 wildfires in northwestern Spain and northern Portugal during August 2025 using satellite observations from the Tropospheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI). Through a plume masking method that exploits the synergy between collocated NO 2 and CO TROPOMI observations in complex multi-fire scenes, we infer CO emission rates for 46 individual hotspots. The area studied represents about 70 % of the total burned area in the Iberian Peninsula during that period. The inferred TROPOMI-based emission rates are compared against three fire emission inventories: the Global Fire Assimilation System (GFAS), the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED) and the Fire Inventory from NCAR (FINN). Our results indicate that inventories systematically underestimate CO emissions by about a factor of 3 relative to TROPOMI-derived estimates, consistent with findings from previous studies on other extreme wildfire events. Additionally, we also investigate the NO x / CO mole density ratio (MDR; NO x = NO + NO 2 ) as a proxy for combustion efficiency. This estimate is obtained from TROPOMI NO 2 / CO MDR using literature-based NO 2 -to-NO x conversion factor. The TROPOMI-derived NO x / CO MDR values are consistently lower than those from inventories, with regional variability suggesting differences in combustion phase and fuel type across the study domain. These results highlight the potential of combined satellite observations to assess wildfire emissions in complex fire scenes, while also pointing to limitations in current fire emission inventories under such conditions.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-15763-2026.title: The boundary of nighttime ozone chemical equilibrium as an indicator of local chemistry disturbances in the polar mesopause region
doi:10.5194/acp-26-15763-2026.summary: The nighttime ozone chemical equilibrium (NOCE) is a key assumption widely employed in various applications within the mesopause region, such as retrieving difficult-to-measure characteristics from observational data. Previously, the NOCE boundary criterion was used to analyze its long-term evolution based on SABER/TIMED data, primarily at low and mid-latitudes. This study extends this focus to polar latitudes. We demonstrate that the NOCE criterion clearly delineates the main features of the transition zone that vertically separates regions of strong and weak diurnal photochemical oscillations of O and H. During the polar night, this transition zone degenerates into a sharp step in the vertical profiles of these species, and the criterion accurately identifies the altitude of this step. Furthermore, we analyze the evolution of the NOCE boundary using SABER/TIMED observations in conjunction with MERRA-2 reanalysis data for the winter–spring periods from 2002 to 2025. We show that the most pronounced variability of the NOCE boundary occurs at northern polar latitudes during and after strong Sudden Stratospheric Warmings accompanied by stratopause elevation events. Prior to or during the onset of such warmings, the daily mean altitude of the boundary can rise to ∼86 km. Following these events, it rapidly descends to 72–74 km, where it can remain for an extended period. Model studies of the 2009 winter show that the NOCE boundary closely tracks the variability of the median vertical distributions of O, as well as the volume emission rates of OH( v =1–9), O( 1 S), and O 2 (b1Σg+).

doi:10.5194/acp-26-15721-2026.title: Organic condensation derived from different volatility parameterizations and its implications for ambient nanoparticle growth
doi:10.5194/acp-26-15721-2026.summary: Atmospheric new particle formation (NPF) supplies up to half of global cloud condensation nuclei, yet the growth of sub-15 nm nanoparticles – the stage most vulnerable to scavenging – remains poorly constrained, largely because the volatility of oxygenated organic molecules (OOMs) is highly uncertain. Using a purpose-built laminar flow reactor that isolates particle–particle coagulation from OOM condensation, we show that six of seven widely used OOM volatility parameterizations substantially overestimate nanoparticle growth rates, with the largest bias under the high-NO x conditions. A recent parameterization constrained by ambient organic aerosol volatility reproduces our laboratory observations across diverse OOM precursors, seed sizes (3–5 nm), and NO x regimes. By applying this laboratory-validated framework to NPF events at Lake Tai, China, in summer 2023, OOM and H 2 SO 4 condensation explain about 53 % of the observed 3–15 nm growth rate, rising to roughly 86 % at the upper bound of the estimated uncertainty in OOM concentrations. This residual is consistent with, but not uniquely attributable to, processes absent from the present framework: incomplete instrumental coverage of condensable vapours, uncertainties in the measured size distributions and growth rates, and simplifications within the growth model may each contribute, and a box-model estimate indicates that heterogeneous gas–particle reactions could account for a substantial part of it. Our results identify a volatility parameterization that performs reliably under NO x -rich conditions and delineate the sensitivities that must be constrained before residual nanoparticle growth can be attributed to specific mechanisms.

doi:10.1029/2026je009951.summary: Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, Volume 131, Issue 11, November 2026. Research Article

doi:10.5194/ar-2026-47.title: Towards a more accurate measurement of particles matter during domestic wood combustion: impact of the sampling point, assessment and chemical characterisation of the condensable fraction
doi:10.5194/ar-2026-47.summary: Towards a more accurate measurement of particles matter during domestic wood combustion: impact of the sampling point, assessment and chemical characterisation of the condensable fraction Clara Akl, Julie Schobing, Cornelius Schönnenbeck, and Gwenaëlle Trouvé Aerosol Research Discuss., https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-2026-47,2026 Preprint under review for AR (discussion: open, 0 comments) European Ecodesign regulation underestimates a major part of the total aerosol at the stack during domestic wood combustion because the condensable fraction (CF) is not taken into account. This study presents a new experimental methodology to quantify CF. The condensable fraction accounts for 50 % at minima of the total concentration of particulate emissions. This is an important result that needs to be included in future experimental protocols of the total aerosol.

doi:10.5194/ar-4-577-2026.title: Measurements of NaCl in ambient air with a capture vaporizer-ToF-ACSM
doi:10.5194/ar-4-577-2026.summary: Sea spray aerosol is important for climate and atmospheric chemistry as it influences radiative forcing and heterogeneous reactions, but few online methods exist for quantifying sub-micron sea spray concentrations. Common chemical speciation instruments, such as aerosol mass spectrometers (AMS) and aerosol chemical speciation monitors (ACSM), are usually not used for sea salt quantification due to the incomplete evaporation of refractory sodium chloride (NaCl). This study evaluates the capability of the time-of-flight-ACSM (ToF-ACSM) equipped with a capture vaporizer (CV) to detect and quantify sea salt aerosol for the first time. Key NaCl marker ions (m/z 23 (Na), m/z 58 (Na 35 Cl), and m/z 60 (Na 37 Cl)) were identified through controlled laboratory calibration. The calibration experiments show that the ACSM response (ions s −1 ) at characteristic NaCl fragments scales with the available particle surface area, yielding a surface-normalized signal that is only weakly dependent on particle size for monodisperse NaCl aerosol. This indicates that the CV-ToF-ACSM provides a direct and robust measure of sea salt aerosol surface area. If a prior estimate of the NaCl size distribution is available, this signal can be converted to aerosol mass concentrations. Furthermore, controlled chamber experiments indicated that secondary organic aerosol (SOA) formed from α -pinene as a precursor and condensed on the NaCl particles does not produce significant quantities of fragments at the m/z values characteristic for NaCl. Field experiments at a coastal site showed that conditions with onshore winds resulted in high correlations ( R 2 = 0.949–0.977) between the three key NaCl marker ions. By applying the laboratory-derived calibration formula to the raw CV-ToF-ACSM m/z 23 signal, sea salt aerosol surface concentrations could be quantitatively determined in real time. However, the slope between the fragments at m/z 23 and m/z 58 is higher in the ambient data than in the laboratory calibration, suggesting reduced Cl relative to Na due to aging reactions of the sea salt particles in the coastal environment. Overall, these results demonstrate that the CV-ToF-ACSM can provide quantitative real-time information on submicron sea salt aerosol before aging, particularly in terms of surface area, while accurate mass concentration retrieval requires additional NaCl size distribution information. These findings highlight the potential to improve the characterization of marine aerosol sources and their role in atmospheric processes.

doi:10.5194/ar-2026-42.title: Sensitivity Analysis for a Statistical Prediction Model Utilized for Particle Number Concentrations with a Focus on Submicron Size Fractions
doi:10.5194/ar-2026-42.summary: Sensitivity Analysis for a Statistical Prediction Model Utilized for Particle Number Concentrations with a Focus on Submicron Size Fractions Adeeb Ktaish, Nahid Atashi, Ola Surakhi, Yu Zhao, Tianyi Zhao, Martha Arbayani Zaidan, Tuukka Petäjä, Tuija Jokinen, Wei Du, Markku Kulmala, and Tareq Hussein Aerosol Research Discuss., https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-2026-42,2026 Preprint under review for AR (discussion: open, 0 comments) We developed a regression model to predict particle number concentrations across size ranges using meteorological variables and trace gases at SMEAR stations in Helsinki, Hyytiälä, and Värriö. The model performed well and captured diurnal and seasonal variability. Five scenarios showed that training data selection, recency, and duration influence performance, with limited benefits from older data. These findings guide training data selection and support future forecasting.

doi:10.5194/ar-4-559-2026.title: Assessment of cabin filtration efficiency: contribution to an on-road methodology
doi:10.5194/ar-4-559-2026.summary: The use of cabin filters provides protection for passengers against outdoor pollution caused by particles (aerosols) when travelling by car. Their filtration efficiency is assessed through rigorous laboratory studies in accordance with standards. However, there are few or no comparable studies conducted under real road conditions using reference particle measurements to complement the laboratory results. In this context, our study aims to contribute to the improvement of on-road aerosol measurement by evaluating cabin filters with gravimetric measurements. To this end, a sampling line upstream of the cabin filter in an area located under the windscreen and a sampling point downstream of the cabin filter on the front seat inside the cabin were designed. The sampling efficiency of the line was calculated using a transdisciplinary work involving computational fluid dynamics, wind tunnel measurements, and numerical methods. The results showed that its sampling efficiency for PM 1 and PM 2.5 (i.e. particles with an aerodynamic diameter of less than 1 and 2.5 µm, respectively) is greater than 94 % and 77 %, respectively. Next, on-road tests were carried out in a moving car in the Paris region for two different cabin filters and during tests without a cabin filter. The average filtration efficiency was 54.4 % ( n = 15), 52.7 % ( n = 14), and 9.5 % ( n = 4) for PM 1 and 57.6 % ( n = 9), 56 % ( n = 9), and 32.0 % ( n = 4) for PM 2.5 , respectively, for filter A and filter B and without a cabin filter. Lastly, optical counters were simultaneously operated with gravimetric measurements. The results showed that optical counters underestimate the mass concentration of PM 2.5 , highlighting the importance of using a reference method to measure the particles under real road conditions.

doi:10.5194/ar-4-547-2026.title: Inhalation of small particles (PM2.5) in urban road tunnels and underground in Madrid (Spain) – a citizen science project
doi:10.5194/ar-4-547-2026.summary: Some public infrastructures do not routinely monitor air pollution, particularly in semi-enclosed transport environments such as road tunnels and metro systems. Low-cost sensors (LCSs) may complement official monitoring by providing accessible exposure data. This study aimed to validate LCS performance and to assess PM 2.5 concentrations in urban transport microenvironments in a large city with the active participation of various citizens. LCS measurements were compared with reference station data using Pearson correlation coefficients. The device was mounted outside a vehicle while driving through road tunnels, and additional measurements were conducted on metro platforms and inside subway carriages. All measurements were carried out by different citizens who had been previously trained. The correlation between LCS and the reference station was high ( r =0.9301; 95 % CI: 0.926–0.934), supporting device reliability. In road tunnels, mean PM 2.5 increased from 12.62 µg m −3 (standard deviation (SD) 11.3) in the first half of the journey to 16.6 µg m −3 (SD 15.2) in the second half ( p <0.001). On metro platforms, concentrations exceeded 10 µg m −3 (mean 20 µg m −3 ; range 10–32), while inside carriages, levels remained above 5 µg m −3 (mean 10 µg m −3 ; range 5.8–17.8). These results have been reviewed, assessed, and discussed by all participating citizens from the signatory associations. As no safe threshold for PM 2.5 exposure has been established, systematic monitoring and the integration of low-cost technologies into public health surveillance are needed to inform regulation and urban transport policies.

doi:10.5194/ar-4-517-2026.title: Measurements and modeling of urban secondary organic aerosol formation potential as a function of precursor volatility class in the Los Angeles area during summer 2022
doi:10.5194/ar-4-517-2026.summary: Urban secondary organic aerosol (SOA) contributes to degraded air quality, which can affect human health. Improvements in Los Angeles (LA), CA, air quality have mainly plateaued since 2010. In summer 2022, measurements were made to quantify the SOA formation potential (SOA-FP) in ambient LA air. Two oxidation flow reactors (OFRs) ingested ambient air: one was equipped with an electrically conductive polymer inlet that denuded lower-volatility species, and the other was run without an inlet. This allowed the separate quantification of SOA-FP from higher- vs. lower-volatility precursors. To our knowledge these are the first direct measurements of these fractions. Measured ambient SOA was similar, and total SOA-FP was lower in 2022 vs. 2010, consistent with higher ambient OH causing greater consumptions of SOA precursors in 2022. The dual-OFR measurements suggest ∼ 31 % of the total SOA-FP is due to compounds with volatilities in the semi-volatile organic compound (SVOC) and lower intermediate-volatility organic compound (IVOC) ranges. Evidence suggests these lower-volatility precursors are mainly from direct emissions, rather than oxidation products from upwind aging. Results are compared to two box models: one based on CRACMM and the other adapted from a recent Caltech publication. CRACMM predicted ambient OA well but underpredicted SOA-FP by about a factor of 2, while the Caltech model underestimated OA and overpredicted SOA-FP by a factor of 2.5. Our study finds terpenoids contribute to, but do not dominate, SOA-FP.

doi:10.5194/ar-2026-39.title: AeroMiG: Multi-modal Inverse-Gamma modeling for aerosol particle number size distributions
doi:10.5194/ar-2026-39.summary: AeroMiG: Multi-modal Inverse-Gamma modeling for aerosol particle number size distributions Abdur Rahman, Juha Kangasluoma, Santtu Mikkonen, Tareq Hussein, Tuukka Petäjä, Sasu Tarkoma, and Martha Arbayani Zaidan Aerosol Research Discuss., https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-2026-39,2026 Preprint under review for AR (discussion: open, 0 comments) PNSDs are vital for aerosol analysis, but traditional log-Gaussian models struggle with asymmetric modes. We introduce AeroMiG, an Inverse-Gamma framework that accurately models overlapping, asymmetric distributions. It models asymmetric and overlapping PNSDs, outperforms log-Gaussian models in speed and accuracy, maintains consistent performance across NPF events, and interprets Inverse-Gamma parameters for modal properties.

doi:10.5194/ar-2026-41.title: Ice nucleating particle flux density estimated with radon tracer methods during conditions dominated by thermally driven mountain winds
doi:10.5194/ar-2026-41.summary: Ice nucleating particle flux density estimated with radon tracer methods during conditions dominated by thermally driven mountain winds Annika Einbock, Franz Conen, Alan D. Griffiths, and Scott D. Chambers Aerosol Research Discuss., https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-2026-41,2026 Preprint under review for AR (discussion: open, 0 comments) Some particles emitted from the Earth’s surface can modify clouds by triggering ice formation, so called ice nucleating particles (INPs). We estimate the flux of biological INPs from the source region of a high-altitude site by applying two new implementations of a method originally developed to determine greenhouse gas fluxes. Initial estimates suggest that transport on fair-weather summer days only makes a relatively small contribution to the annual export of biological INPs above the Alps.

doi:10.5194/ar-4-501-2026.title: Stability and composition of large sulfuric acid–methanesulfonic acid–base molecular clusters
doi:10.5194/ar-4-501-2026.summary: Sulfuric acid (SA), together with base molecules such as ammonia (AM), methylamine (MA), and dimethylamine (DMA), is known to play a central role in atmospheric new particle formation (NPF). NPF occurs through gas-to-particle conversion via the formation and growth of molecular clusters. While previous studies have demonstrated that mixtures of bases can strongly enhance nucleation rates, the influence of multiple acidic species for larger cluster stability and growth remains less explored. In this work, we investigate the role of mixed-acid systems in atmospheric cluster formation using quantum chemical calculations, assisted by machine learning. Cluster structures containing SA, methanesulfonic acid (MSA), and atmospherically relevant bases (AM, MA, and DMA), with compositions up to 10 acid–base pairs, were generated through extensive configurational sampling using ABCluster and metadynamics simulations with CREST. The resulting structures were subsequently optimized at the B97-3c level of theory, while a PaiNN machine-learning model was used to accelerate the calculation. Our results show that, in contrast to previously reported base synergy, the acid synergy between SA and MSA is weak and highly system dependent. SA consistently dominates the thermodynamic stability of the smallest clusters, and MSA-only acid–base interactions are insufficient to explain efficient initial particle formation. In particular, for systems involving DMA, the strong SA–DMA interaction governs the cluster energetics, with little contribution of MSA to the stability. However, MSA can influence cluster stability at larger sizes in systems involving weaker bases such as AM and MA, especially under conditions where the relative abundance of MSA is high. These findings indicate that MSA acts not as a primary nucleating acid but rather as a secondary species that participates in the early growth of clusters. Overall, this work highlights that the roles of different atmospheric acids in NPF are fundamentally distinct: SA controls the initial nucleation step, whereas MSA may enhance subsequent cluster growth under specific atmospheric conditions.

doi:10.5194/ar-4-485-2026.title: Iberulite fall and formation mechanism during a Sahara dust event in Switzerland in February 2021
doi:10.5194/ar-4-485-2026.summary: Iberulite fall and formation mechanism during a Sahara dust event in Switzerland in February 2021 Bernard Grobety, Philippe Favreau, Juanita Rausch, David Jaramillo-Vogel, Martin Steinbacher, and Christoph Neururer Aerosol Research, 4, 485–500, https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-4-485-2026, 2026 The iberulite fall was, to our knowledge, the first reported in central Europe. What was special was that the fall was observed in situ and that the meteorological conditions during the fall are well known. The meteorology and the particle size distribution inside the iberulites strongly corroborate below-cloud scavenging as a probable formation mechanism. The discovery of further iberulites Saharan dust event (SDE) samples collected since suggests that iberulites are common but overlooked by other researchers.

doi:10.5194/ar-2026-35.title: Chemical Speciation and Source Apportionment of PM2.5 in Greek Urban and Suburban Areas: Insights from the PANACEA Initiative
doi:10.5194/ar-2026-35.summary: Chemical Speciation and Source Apportionment of PM2.5 in Greek Urban and Suburban Areas: Insights from the PANACEA Initiative Stefanos Papagiannis, Evangelia Diapouli, Vasiliki Vasilatou, Maria Gini, Konstantinos Kourtidis, Christos Kaltsonoudis, Maria Tsagkaraki, Georgios Grivas, Eleni Liakakou, Αikaterini Bougiatioti, Nikolaos Mihalopoulos, and Konstantinos Eleftheriadis Aerosol Research Discuss., https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-2026-35,2026 Preprint under review for AR (discussion: open, 3 comments) This study investigated fine particulate air pollution across five Greek cities to identify its primary sources. By chemically analyzing over 545 24-hour air filter samples, we mapped seasonal patterns and identified seven major emission sources. Marked differences show that while regional background pollution strongly affects PM2.5 levels, local activities, particularly winter wood burning for residential heating, remain a primary cause of urban air degradation in Greece.

doi:10.5194/ar-4-457-2026.title: Drivers governing the seasonality of new particle formation in the Arctic
doi:10.5194/ar-4-457-2026.summary: Drivers governing the seasonality of new particle formation in the Arctic Dominic Heslin-Rees, Peter Tunved, Diego Aliaga, Janne Lampilahti, Ilona Riipinen, Annica M. L. Ekman, Ki-Tae Park, Martina Mazzini, Stefania Gilardoni, Roseline Thakur, Kihong Park, Young Jun Yoon, Kitack Lee, Mikko Sipilä, Mauro Mazzola, and Radovan Krejci Aerosol Research, 4, 457–483, https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-4-457-2026, 2026 New particles form in the atmosphere and can influence the climate. We studied Arctic new particle formation (NPF) from 2022 to 2024 at the Zeppelin Observatory, on Svalbard. NPF occurs from April to November, peaking in late spring as sunlight increases. Some particles measured on-site grow large enough to seed clouds. Sunlight and existing aerosol particles strongly impact the likelihood of NPF, which mainly originates from marine regions, particularly the Greenland Sea.

doi:10.5194/ar-4-441-2026.title: Dispersion normalisation method for improved long-term trend evaluation: heavy metals in ambient air in the Czech Republic, Central Europe (2010–2021)
doi:10.5194/ar-4-441-2026.summary: Dispersion normalisation method for improved long-term trend evaluation: heavy metals in ambient air in the Czech Republic, Central Europe (2010–2021) Adéla Holubová Šmejkalová, Radek Lhotka, Hana Škáchová, and Jan Pacner Aerosol Research, 4, 441–456, https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-4-441-2026, 2026 This research examined whether legislative measures to reduce heavy metal pollution have been effective in the Czech Republic. We analysed 12 years of data from 16 monitoring stations and used a method that reduces the influence of changing weather. The results showed that this method is suitable for evaluating long-term trends and helps avoid errors in interpreting pollution levels affected by year-to-year weather differences.

doi:10.5194/ar-2026-33.title: A metrological calibration facility for particle number counters used in emission measurements
doi:10.5194/ar-2026-33.summary: A metrological calibration facility for particle number counters used in emission measurements Anza Waheed, Jorge Saturno, Arpit Malik, Johannes Rosahl, Sonja Pratzler, and Andreas Nowak Aerosol Research Discuss., https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-2026-33,2026 Preprint under review for AR (discussion: final response, 2 comments) Vehicle exhaust contains ultrafine soot particles that can harm health and the environment. Particle number measurements are essential because these particles contribute little to particulate mass. PTB developed a calibration facility producing stable soot particles of defined sizes for testing particle counters. Instruments are compared with a reference linked to national standards. The facility improves measurement accuracy and comparability between laboratories and supporting authorities.

doi:10.5194/ar-2026-32.title: Chemical composition of indoor and outdoor particles in a building near an international airport: Influence of local and long-range transported air pollution
doi:10.5194/ar-2026-32.summary: Chemical composition of indoor and outdoor particles in a building near an international airport: Influence of local and long-range transported air pollution Sami D. Harni, Delun Li, Ville Silvonen, Laura Salo, Teemu Lepistö, Toni Tykkä, Mohamed Elsayed, Luis Barreira, Sanna Saarikoski, Ilpo Kulmala, Jarkko V. Niemi, Heidi Hellén, Arto Säämänen, Topi Rönkkö, and Hilkka Timonen Aerosol Research Discuss., https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-2026-32,2026 Preprint under review for AR (discussion: final response, 3 comments) In this study, indoor and outdoor pollutant concentrations were measured in a mechanically ventilated building in the immediate vicinity of a busy international airport. The measurement period included a strong long-range transport event. Clear differences in indoor outdoor ratios were observed between different pollutants and between normal and long-range transport periods. This study highlights the significance of a intake filtration system in indoor pollutant concentration management.

doi:10.5194/ar-4-429-2026.title: Look-up tables for complex refractive index correction of particle sizes measured by common research-grade optical particle counters
doi:10.5194/ar-4-429-2026.summary: Look-up tables for complex refractive index correction of particle sizes measured by common research-grade optical particle counters Paola Formenti and Claudia Di Biagio Aerosol Research, 4, 429–440, https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-4-429-2026, 2026 This study improves the accuracy of optical particle counters (OPCs), instruments used to measure airborne particles important for air quality and climate research. Because OPC measurements depend not only on particle size but also on composition and shape, results can be uncertain. The paper provides a standardized database of correction factors for five commercial OPCs, helping researchers produce more reliable and consistent aerosol measurements across a wide range of atmospheric conditions.

doi:10.5194/ar-2026-31.title: Complex refractive indices of flame soot from different combustion conditions retrieved using Mie and RDG-FA theories: a simulation chamber study
doi:10.5194/ar-2026-31.summary: Complex refractive indices of flame soot from different combustion conditions retrieved using Mie and RDG-FA theories: a simulation chamber study Johannes Heuser, Claudia Di Biagio, Jérôme Yon, Mathieu Cazaunau, Antonin Bergé, Edouard Pangui, Marco Zanatta, Laura Renzi, Angela Marinoni, Chenjie Yu, Servanne Chevaillier, Daniel Ferry, Michel Maillé, Paola Formenti, Benedicte Picquet-Varrault, and Jean-François Doussin Aerosol Research Discuss., https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-2026-31,2026 Preprint under review for AR (discussion: open, 0 comments) We retrieve refractive indices of laboratory-generated soot from measured particle properties using Mie and RDG-FA optical calculations, and quantify uncertainties via Monte Carlo simulations. The inferred refractive indices strongly depend on the theory employed, highlighting the need for consistency between optical theory and refractive index. Mie retrievals are sensitive to coagulation and size growth, while RDG-FA retrievals depend strongly on the uncertainty of assumed particle morphology.

doi:10.5194/ar-4-413-2026.title: Coral reef exposure increases aerosol and cloud condensation nuclei over the Great Barrier Reef
doi:10.5194/ar-4-413-2026.summary: Coral reef exposure increases aerosol and cloud condensation nuclei over the Great Barrier Reef Juha Sulo, Magdalena Okuljar, Joel Alroe, Zijun Li, Eva Johanna Horchler, Luke Cravigan, Branka Miljevic, Luke Harrison, Daniel Harrison, and Zoran Ristovski Aerosol Research, 4, 413–427, https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-4-413-2026, 2026 The Great Barrier Reef is the world’s largest coral reef system, and the air above it plays a role in cloud formation. Using direct measurements taken over several years, this study shows that although the reef has low aerosol concentrations, air that passes directly over coral reefs contains more very small particles, providing the first direct evidence that reefs add particles to the atmosphere. These locally produced particles make a measurable contribution to cloud formation over the reef.

doi:10.5194/ar-4-397-2026.title: Atmospheric new particle formation enhanced by tricarboxylic acids
doi:10.5194/ar-4-397-2026.summary: Atmospheric new particle formation enhanced by tricarboxylic acids Astrid Nørskov Pedersen, Yosef Knattrup, and Jonas Elm Aerosol Research, 4, 397–411, https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-4-397-2026, 2026 We investigated the new particle formation (NPF) potential of three atmospherically relevant oxygenated organic molecules (OOMs) using high-level computational methods. Cluster thermodynamics and formation rates were evaluated for systems containing sulfuric acid and various nitrogen bases. All three OOMs enhanced cluster formation, with dimethylamine-containing clusters showing the greatest effect. Pinyl diaterpenylic ester formed the most stable clusters due to its molecular flexibility.

doi:10.5194/ar-4-373-2026.title: Challenges in measuring sticky biogenic ice-nucleating macromolecules
doi:10.5194/ar-4-373-2026.summary: Challenges in measuring sticky biogenic ice-nucleating macromolecules Joseph Robinson, Martin I. Daily, Polly B. Foster, Jack P. Macklin, James B. McQuaid, Mark D. Tarn, and Benjamin J. Murray Aerosol Research, 4, 373–396, https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-4-373-2026, 2026 Ice formation in many clouds is initiated by airborne particles, which are often measured by collecting them on a filter and washing them into water for analysis. Using controlled laboratory experiments, we show that some of these particles adhere strongly to the filter and are not recovered. As a result, this common method can underestimate how many ice-forming particles are present in the atmosphere.

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-space-.title: Space dust particles point to ancient heavy-oxygen water reservoir in the Kuiper belt
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-space-.summary: Way out past the asteroid belt, another belt encircles the planets in our solar system. The Kuiper belt, beyond Neptune, preserves icy bodies that escaped much of the processing experienced by objects closer to the sun. Unlike the rocky and metallic asteroid belt, Kuiper belt objects are composed mostly of frozen water, methane and ammonia, mixed with rock and dust. Astrobiology

Planetary Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-simula.title: Simulated moon dust turned into LEGO-like blocks for settlements
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-simula.summary: Permanent structures on the moon could start with something already there: lunar dust. url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-subaru.title: Subaru Telescope reveals the shape and temperature of Comet Encke's nucleus
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-subaru.summary: Mid-infrared observations with the Subaru Telescope have revealed the shape and surface temperature of the nucleus of Comet 2P/Encke. By analyzing how the nucleus's thermal emission changed as it rotated, the researchers found that the nucleus is elongated, with a long axis of about 7 kilometers and a short axis of about 3 kilometers. They also determined that the surface temperature at the time of observation was 328 ± 7 Kelvin (about 55°C). Planetary Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-earth-.title: Earth's gravity may have kept the early moon's volcanic heart beating
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-earth-.summary: We typically think of the moon as a static, floating object that has remained the same for basically its entire lifetime, with an occasional asteroid impact serving as an exception. That understanding is grounded in physics—the moon should have cooled rapidly after forming when a huge protoplanet hit the early Earth around 4.5 billion years ago. But some lunar material returned from the Chang'e-5 mission was notably formed only around 2 billion years ago, yet appeared to be volcanic in origin. Planetary Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-martia.summary: Mars shares many landforms and weather patterns with Earth, including changing seasons, volcanoes, canyons, dust storms, dust devils and water ice. These are among each planet's striking features, but the major difference is that Earth's polar ice caps are both composed of water, while Mars' north polar ice cap is composed only of water and its southern polar ice cap is carbon dioxide. doi:10.3847/psj/aeb6be.title: Surface-based Geophysical Monitoring of Conductive Planetary Environments: Integrated Electrical-resistivity-imaging–Electromagnetic-induction Approach
doi:10.3847/psj/aeb6be.summary: Abstract Planetary habitability assessments have relied heavily on detecting subsurface liquid water, while redox gradients are also key for identifying energy sources in extreme environments. Currently, extraterrestrial subsurface characterization exhibits a critical scale gap between broad-scale orbital datasets and localized, invasive rover sampling. Ground-penetrating radar (GPR) serves as the primary method bridging this gap, but signals experience severe attenuation in conductive environments that are astrobiologically significant. To address these instrumental limitations, we propose a geoelectrical framework that provides subsurface-conductivity information relevant to habitability assessments. This methodology relies on calibrated electromagnetic-induction (EMI) spatial surveys with electrical-resistivity-imaging (ERI) surveys. We tested the framework during seasonal deployments at Zodletone Spring, Oklahoma, a methane-bearing, euxinic, saline planetary analog. Calibrated EMI surveys resolved highly conductive smectite-rich clays and a conductivity anomaly coincident with the independently identified redox transition zone. These observations provide the first evidence that seasonal processes can drive large electrical-conductivity changes (>1000 mS m −1 ) detectable by EMI in situ and confirmed through ground-truth monitoring. The anomalies are confined to surface smectite-rich clays and covary with seasonal thermal and hydrological dynamics. Building on these field constraints, a conceptual modeling framework shows that, under idealized assumptions, EMI can also theoretically detect temporal fluctuations within hypothesized Martian ice-brine lenses. Together, the field and modeling results demonstrate a noninvasive geophysical workflow that accurately quantifies shallow subsurface variability in extreme environments. Integrating this framework into planetary missions will provide contextual information relevant to habitability and help optimize target selection prior to invasive sampling.

doi:10.3847/psj/aeb2ee.title: Primordial and Radiogenic Argon 40 in Uranus and Neptune
doi:10.3847/psj/aeb2ee.summary: Abstract The atmospheric abundance of 40 Ar in Uranus and Neptune has been proposed as a tracer of their rocky component through the radioactive decay of 40 K. However, the primordial 40 Ar contribution remains poorly constrained because argon incorporation into planetary building blocks varied across the protosolar nebula through condensation and clathration. We investigate the relative contributions of primordial and radiogenic sources to atmospheric 40 Ar and assess the conditions under which this isotope can constrain the formation environment or rocky component of Uranus and Neptune. We combine calculations of radiogenic 40 Ar production with a time-dependent thermochemical model of the protosolar nebula that follows the condensation, clathration, and transport of Ar-bearing species. Combining atmospheric carbon enrichments inferred from CH 4 measurements with modeled variations in the Ar/C ratio of solids yields primordial 40 Ar enrichments of ∼1–610 times protosolar in Uranus and ∼1–1220 times protosolar in Neptune, depending on the formation location and epoch of their building blocks relative to the Ar clathration front and ice line. Such enrichments can overwhelm the radiogenic component. Consequently, atmospheric 40 Ar may constrain the rocky component when the primordial contribution is small and sufficient interior-to-atmosphere transport has occurred. When the primordial contribution is large, 40 Ar instead primarily traces the thermochemical conditions under which the building blocks formed. Future measurements of 40 Ar together with 36 Ar, N/H, 15 N/ 14 N, 13 C/ 12 C, and below-cloud C/H would provide complementary constraints on the formation environment and the nature of the accreted volatile and refractory reservoirs.

doi:10.3847/psj/aeb417.title: Geomorphic Evidence for Ice-rich Mass Wasting in Ceres’ Polar Craters
doi:10.3847/psj/aeb417.summary: Abstract Ceres’ current low obliquity permits the existence of permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) near the poles. A small fraction of the hundreds of shadowed craters on Ceres contain bright crater floor deposits (BCFDs) inferred to be water ice, but the origin of the bright material and the role of PSRs in Ceres’ cryospheric evolution remain poorly understood. We performed a comprehensive mapping survey of BCFDs in polar craters, finding that the total bright area is ∼7 km 2 , comparable to the extent of surficial ice exposures on Ceres globally. The morphology of the bright material in two PSRs is indicative of mass wasting, suggesting that locally derived ice-rich material might be exposed in polar craters rather than all bright material being the result of atmospheric capture. Since all craters at high latitudes preserve ice in the near surface, mass wasting might be a ubiquitous process in the interiors of small craters, resulting in widespread modification of their topography. We measured depth-to-diameter ratios and interior slopes for thousands of simple craters and find that crater depth is negatively correlated with latitude. Extrapolating this trend to the poles, where the reliability of topographic data is low, predicts that kilometer-scale craters near the poles are shallower than those at the equator by hundreds of meters. Based on the observed shallowing of simple craters at high latitudes, even outside areas where persistent shadowing occurs, PSRs on present-day Ceres are likely subject to thermal or volatile-driven processes not present on other airless bodies.

doi:10.3847/psj/aeb37d.title: The Limits of Tidal Circularization and Atmospheric Escape for Mini-Neptunes and Super-Earths: The Case of TOI-2257 b
doi:10.3847/psj/aeb37d.summary: Abstract With a 35 day orbital period and ∼0.5 eccentricity, TOI-2257 b occupies a sparsely populated corner of transiting mini-Neptune parameter space and may lie near the orbital distance at which tidal and atmospheric escape processes become negligible. To test this hypothesis, we performed simulations of the combined stellar, tidal, and atmospheric evolution and confirmed that TOI-2257 b does lie near this boundary, regardless of whether it formed with or without a primordial hydrogen envelope. In the mini-Neptune scenario, we find that all cases retain an envelope of at least 0.02 M ⊕ for 8 Gyr, but that the envelope mass can be halved if it was initially larger than 0.2 M ⊕ . We find that tidal evolution only occurs for cases with initial envelope masses larger than 0.02 M ⊕ because their radii are large enough to generate significant torques. In the super-Earth scenario, the planet could lose ∼10 Earth ocean masses of surface water during the ∼75 Myr pre-main sequence and therefore could be habitable if it formed with ≳2× Earth’s surface water mass. The predicted tidal heating surface flux tends to be similar to Io, with no cases approaching the flux required to drive a runaway greenhouse. We find that if the planet is rocky, then eccentricities larger than 0.62 today are strongly disfavored, implying that larger eccentricities could confirm the gaseous nature of the planet. These results suggest that TOI-2257 b could provide valuable constraints on mini-Neptune properties and new insight into the radius valley shape as a function of eccentricity.

doi:10.3847/psj/aea909.title: New Insights into Venus’s Volatile Cycles Revealed by the Formation of Magnesite and Fluoro–Micas
doi:10.3847/psj/aea909.summary: Venus’ surface chemistry and mineralogy remain poorly constrained. Understanding surface–atmosphere interactions under a simulated Venus environment can be used to predict Venus’s surface composition and its past and current volatile cycles. This includes identifying minerals that could provide evidence for past or subsurface water. We exposed six rock-forming minerals in the Glenn Extreme Environment Rig (GEER) to simulated Venusian conditions. Magnesite formed from brucite by dehydration and carbonization. Phlogopite and muscovite reacted with HF to form fluorophlogopite and fluoromuscovite, respectively, which demonstrates in situ OH-F substitution under simulated Venusian conditions. Since fluorine substitution can increase the thermal stability of micas, this reaction may help preserve hydrous minerals that formed during an earlier, water-rich period of Venus’ history. Assuming Earth-like volcanic outgassing rates and no removal mechanisms since Venus’ last major resurfacing (∼500 Mya), SO2 and HF abundances could increase by several percent. Our experimental results and thermodynamic analyses reaffirm continuous emplacement of fresh volcanic material and sustained outgassing of volcanic gas to maintain the current atmospheric abundances. Identifying magnesite and fluoro-micas on the surface of Venus could provide indicators about current volatile cycles and Venus’ past geological and atmospheric evolution.

doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11241-9.title: Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*
doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11241-9.summary: Abstract A new epoch for direct visualization of accretion dynamics near the event horizon of a black hole began when the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration synthesized an Earth-sized aperture with millimetre radio interferometry and published the first reconstructed image 1–4 of a black hole shadow at the core of radio galaxy Messier 87 (M87). The image appeared as a ring-like structure, representing the gravitationally lensed and redshifted emission around the central supermassive black hole, M87*, located at the galactic nucleus. However, application of various data analysis and imaging heuristics resulted in divergent representations of M87* fine-scale features 3,5–7 , with some external analyses even challenging the fundamental ring-like morphology of the source 8,9 . Such difficulties arise as a consequence of the inherent sparsity of the very long baseline interferometry measurements, making interferometric image reconstruction an inadequately constrained problem. Moreover, the solution is sensitive to instrument calibration, post-processing algorithms and imaging hyperparameters. Here we apply an independent imaging algorithm that we have developed to the M87* dataset that is free from prescriptive morphological priors and founded on observables immune to instrument calibration errors. We reconstruct the black hole shadow image and unequivocally reproduce a ring-like morphology, with an angular diameter of 42.2 ± 1.5 μas corresponding to a black hole mass of 6.5 ± 0.5 billion solar masses assuming nominal scaling parameters, observed at an inclination angle of approximately 20° from the approaching jet.

doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11285-x.title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife
doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11285-x.summary: Abstract Plastic pollution is a defining feature of the Anthropocene 1 , and microplastics are dispersed by air and water into even remote terrestrial habitats 2–7 , yet the ecological and landscape-level processes that shape microplastic accumulation in terrestrial ecosystems remain poorly understood. Human land-use change is rapidly transforming landscapes worldwide, but the influence of this expanding human footprint on the microplastic burdens in wildlife remains largely unknown. This knowledge gap is particularly pressing in regions that are facing escalating environmental pressures, such as Brazil. Here we pair in vivo microplastic measurements with high-resolution tracking data from lowland tapirs and giant anteaters across Brazil and show that the microplastic burdens carried by free-ranging mammals increase with both the magnitude of their human footprint exposure and their proximity to development and waste management infrastructure. Microplastics were also detected in the blood of individuals occupying seemingly pristine habitats far from development, suggesting that direct exposure to human-modified landscapes is unlikely to be the sole driver of systemic microplastic burdens. In a period of accelerating global land-use change, these findings reveal how individual habitat use and anthropogenic land-use change interact to shape wildlife exposure to microplastics and suggest that managing animals’ proximity to development and waste management infrastructure may reduce the microplastic burdens carried by terrestrial wildlife.

doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11278-w.title: Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines
doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11278-w.summary: Abstract The global transition towards sustainable energy systems has identified tidal power as a uniquely predictable and substantial renewable energy resource 1 . However, the highly unsteady sea environment subjects turbines to severe hydrodynamic loads, greatly increasing capital and maintenance costs 2,3 . Large-scale state-of-the-art turbines at present rely on complex, expensive active pitch systems to mitigate these fluctuations. Here we present a reliable, passive alternative: flexible rubber blades featuring chordwise trailing-edge deformation. We experimentally demonstrate that these flexible blades achieve an equivalent total energy yield over simulated tidal cycles compared with rigid blades with active pitch control, while mitigating high-frequency fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third. This passive load regulation arises from aeroelastic deformation that flattens blade camber under load, enabling structural robustness without added mechanical complexity. These findings suggest that chordwise-flexible blades can enhance the durability and performance of tidal turbines, offering a promising pathway towards more reliable and cost-effective tidal energy generation.
